subsubtopic: DECLARATION TO STRENGTHEN COMMONWEALTH TIES- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to ask the unanimous consent of the House on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity relating to Canada and the Commonwealth.
In light of the fact that today, March 12, has been declared Commonwealth Day, in view of the importance of the Commonwealth as a cornerstone in Canada's external policy, and because of the important role the Commonwealth can and ought to play in world affairs, not to mention the importance of the heads of government meeting to be held in Lusaka next August, I move, seconded by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker):
That this House confirm Canada's deep attachment to the Commonwealth and its determination to take all steps that will strengthen the ties between the countries of this unique international organization.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: CEREMONIES IN RECOGNITION OF COMMONWEALTH DAY
speechtext:
Before beginning question period, may I invite hon. members to join with me in calling attention to the fact that today has been designated Commonwealth Day. This is an annual event which hon. members will know owes its origin to a Canadian proposal, made during the 1975 Heads of Government Meeting, that the second Monday in March should be so designated in order to underline in Canada and in all other Commonwealth countries the importance that we attach to this unique association of 40 countries of great diversity in terms of size, race, colour, creed and culture, and at all stages of economic development.
Oral Questions
Across Canada, special programs have been planned today, especially in schools and public libraries, to mark this special occasion. Yesterday, special interfaith services were held in various centres across this country to mark Commonwealth Day in Canada. Hon. members will have observed the display of flags of all the Commonwealth nations in Confederation Square. This evening, all members of this House are guests at a special reception hosted by the Commonwealth High Commissioners, in co-operation with the Speakers of both Houses, in the Confederation Room in the West Block to mark this very important occasion.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO COUNTER RISING FOOD PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The minister is quoted as having said a month ago, "I hope we can announce certain new measures shortly"-to counter rising food prices. Since that time we have had the announcement of the National Commission on Inflation, and nothing else.
Could the minister tell the House, now, since he promised a month ago that he would be introducing these measures shortly, what these measures are and why they have not been introduced?

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO COUNTER RISING FOOD PRICES
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition is correct; we did announce the establishment of the National Commission on Inflation. I also announced we were bringing back a new, revised competition bill to replace Bill C-13 which was tabled during the last session. Further, I believe the Minister of Agriculture and some of the people responsible for marketing boards did announce increased production quotas for 1979, and the government increased beef quotas by seven million pounds.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO COUNTER RISING FOOD PRICES
speechtext: Outside the House, the minister was quoted as saying he was planning a three-pronged attack on prices. As part of that three-pronged attack he indicated the government would come up with measures to deal with supply shortages and bottlenecks. What specific proposals does the government intend to make to deal with supply shortages and bottlenecks?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO COUNTER RISING FOOD PRICES
speechtext:
These measures will be announced by the responsible ministers in due course. The supply situation is continually under review, as I mentioned in my first answer to the Leader of the Opposition. Some production quotas have already been increased for 1979 as against 1978, but the

ministers responsible for the different food producing sectors will be reviewing these things and making announcements when appropriate. I understand there will be further announcements in this respect during the coming week.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO COUNTER RISING FOOD PRICES
speechtext:
For five years now, ever since the Speech from the Throne which opened this over-long parliament, the minister and the government have been proposing a national food strategy. A month ago, the minister said he would be proposing certain specific measures. Now he says there may be various proposals coming from other ministers at some date in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO COUNTER RISING FOOD PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the national food strategy was never intended to culminate in an announcement at one time. It was a process whereby the many departments in the federal government concerned with food, and in the provincial governments, would get together and work out policies which would be announced from time to time. subtopic: PRODUCTION INCENTIVES FOR FISHERMEN AND FARMERS

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: PRODUCTION INCENTIVES FOR FISHERMEN AND FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister surely knows this is a subject which concerns all Canadians-the rise in prices and the failure of the government to do anything about them.
One of the things the minister said outside the House in the course of his cruel, ongoing deception of the Canadian consumer was that the government proposed to bring in measures to provide new incentives to fishermen and farmers to increase production. Will the minister tell us precisely what new production incentives he is talking about?

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: PRODUCTION INCENTIVES FOR FISHERMEN AND FARMERS
speechtext:
I have already answered that question. I said there were policies announced from time to time dealing with the supply of food. I stated clearly that the major problem with respect to food prices is, in a sense, beyond the control of the government inasmuch as we must buy a good deal of our food in the winter time from abroad. Consequently, to a certain extent we are stuck with the difference in the value of our dollar as compared to the value of foreign currencies.
The other major cause of increased food prices has to do with the beef cycle; because beef prices were very low a few years ago, we are now faced with short supplies and higher prices. In the long run, we hope to work with the producers to make sure we get more stable production and better prices for both consumers and producers.

subtopic: PRODUCTION INCENTIVES FOR FISHERMEN AND FARMERS
speechtext:
This kind of ongoing gobbledegook on the part of the minister is doing nothing to relieve the minds of the people.
Let me ask him this. He has placed great emphasis on phase two of the competition bill which has been dragged out in front of parliament every time an election scare is on. The Prime Minister has said that this parliament will not have time to deal with it. In view of the fact that the new National Commission on Inflation has not been given any guidelines by the government, and in view of the fact that phase two of the competition policy cannot be brought in until the next parliament, what steps does the minister intend to take when he is faced with evidence of price gouging or profiteering which reflects badly on the producers of this country and which, in fact, is causing great concern in the marketplace in the absence of guidelines? Does the minister have any guidelines? What, in his estimation, is profiteering and price gouging?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: PRODUCTION INCENTIVES FOR FISHERMEN AND FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have never said that the reform of competition laws would be a short-term solution to the high prices we are experiencing now, but I did say in my remarks in the House that in the long run the guarantee of fair prices in the marketplace would be an open and competitive marketplace.
With respect to the comments of the hon. member, he and his party last week had an opportunity to put forward their proposals with respect to food prices when the New Democratic Party put its motion before the House. The official opposition had nothing to suggest but that we call an election. I think the hon. member's response to high food prices is to bluster and to make a lot of noise.

subtopic: PRODUCTION INCENTIVES FOR FISHERMEN AND FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of this country would certainly welcome an election so that they could get rid of this tired, worn-out government. If the minister wants proof of that, all he has to do is go to any supermarket check-out counter on any Saturday afternoon and he will get the message loud and clear. This do-nothing minister has assumed responsibility outside this House, but then tries to shrug it off inside.
When can we expect some action from this government, which promised action when it opened this parliament in 1974 when it promised incentives and an adequate return to producers and fair prices to consumers? We had a strategy on food prices last February. When are we going to get some action from this government?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: PRODUCTION INCENTIVES FOR FISHERMEN AND FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously the hon. member does not understand very well, but I said that in the short-run, especially with imported fruits and vegetables, nothing can be done. Nothing much can be done in the short-term with respect to those other than to have a good information program which would help Canadians understand that there are many good, nutritional alternatives available which are much cheaper.
Our department led the way in encouraging the introduction of no-name generic foods which are a good price saving with

respect to many foods, and also the development of no-frills stores which are also a very innovative development which will help bring down food prices. There are many other things and I would be glad to discuss them with the hon. member.

subsubtopic: ONTARIO DOCTORS WITHDRAWING FROM OHIP- CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCE ON MEDICARE PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to say that there are also nutritional alternatives to this government.
My question also deals with the problem of prices, but it is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. It deals with the price of medical care in Ontario. It arises from certain questions which my leader asked the Prime Minister, in the absence of the minister, on Friday.
The minister knows that both the Medical Care Act and the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act of Canada provide certain clear criteria for federal contributions to provincial medical care programs. We know that Canadians must have equal access to medical care and that no charges can impede this access either directly or indirectly. In view of the number of doctors who are leaving the plan to charge higher fees, will the minister agree to meet immediately with those responsible for the medicare plan in Ontario to see that it meets these requirements of federal law?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ONTARIO DOCTORS WITHDRAWING FROM OHIP- CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCE ON MEDICARE PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the last six months or so we have observed different signs that the medical care plan may be eroding. It is surely very fragile right now. I am not referring only to Ontario. I am also thinking of talk of deterrent fees. Other provinces have been testing public opinion in that regard. Of course, we are witnessing the opting out of physicians in Ontario. In Ontario, 17.9 per cent of the physicians have opted out of the medical care program. I have instructed my department to develop guidelines, through consultations with provinces and to make the results of these discussions public, with a view to defining where barriers have developed which prevent access to medicare for Canadians.
I also want to say that on the agenda of last week's meeting of March 6 and 7 of all the deputy ministers of health in Canada, this question was thoroughly studied. I want to reassure everybody that, of course, the federal government will not see eroded the benefits which Canadians derive and enjoy under the national medicare program.

subsubtopic: ONTARIO DOCTORS WITHDRAWING FROM OHIP- CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCE ON MEDICARE PLAN
speechtext:
My supplementary question to the minister is this. In Ontario, the number of doctors leaving the plan has increased by at least 40 per cent. As the minister has just said, this departure of doctors from OHIP not only takes the gut out of medical care but also represents an inflationary attack on
Oral Questions
patients because patients are now paying $600 or $700 for operations and only getting about $400 or $450 from OHIP.
My question to the minister is this: What do these surcharges do to the principle of fairness and to free access to medical care for all Canadians, and what will she do about it apart from simply carrying on investigations and consultations with the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ONTARIO DOCTORS WITHDRAWING FROM OHIP- CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCE ON MEDICARE PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to underline that the situation is serious. So far as I know, it is one of the most serious situations for social security in all of Canada. For instance, Alberta, so far as I know, did not have an opting out provision and extra billing but has now permitted it. That is very dangerous in terms of eventually breaching the universality and accessibility of medicare for all Canadians. The hon. member might think this is a very easy question to solve, but Ontario does not have information to describe what that extra billing represents on which only partial information exists up to now.
As I have said-perhaps I did not put it clearly enough-I have instructed my department not to wait for the provinces to give us that data. Instead, we should seek out all information we need directly to decide whether, yes or no, it is time to withhold payments and eventually give notices to provinces.

subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES DEFICIT-INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT WILL TAKE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. As the deficit relating to goods and services reached a record level of $8.73 billion in 1978 and economists are generally predicting a deficit of over $9 billion in 1979, I want to ask the following question: As Canada's prosperity depends on our capacity to produce new technologies to improve the competitiveness of our industry, but since, as the deficit relating to goods and services indicates, we are losing ground in this area would the minister explain what he intends to do to correct that situation?

subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES DEFICIT-INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT WILL TAKE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we expect an improvement in the situation with time because as the hon. member may realize, the trade surplus increased considerably from $2.9 billion to $3.5 billion last year. For the month of January of this year alone, we had an increase of $100 million. We are also hoping the tourist deficit we have been experiencing for the last several years is going to improve. The growth of these deficits was arrested in the last part of the year and the more competitive Canadian dollar gives us reason to hope that the deficit will start to come down in that area in 1979. So I believe the situation will improve in coming years. We are confident our new competitive position on world markets is going to help us considerably with our trade surplus, and at this time the high level of our balance of payments is not alarming when related to gross national income. The proportions are generally the same as in past years.

subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES DEFICIT-INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT WILL TAKE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to hear the minister because he is always optimistic when he talks about the deficit but at the end of the year we note that his forecasts are always proven wrong. That is regrettable. While there is general agreement to identify the deficit for goods and services with a poor technological performance why is the government constantly reducing its support for research and development as that sector could probably restore, at least in part, a positive balance with respect to goods and services?

subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES DEFICIT-INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT WILL TAKE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should know that the last two budgets that I gave in this House considerably increased tax incentives for research and development and that my colleague, the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers, is now conducting a study with all departments to increase the efficiency of the services provided by the Canadian government to industries and universities for scientific research. I know that in the last few years the government has made considerable efforts to promote research and development in the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES DEFICIT-INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT WILL TAKE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is once again unfounded optimism since the OECD clearly shows that Canada has one of the lowest rates of participation in research and development among its member countries, with a fantastic yearly contribution of 1 per cent of its gross national product.

subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES DEFICIT-INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT WILL TAKE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have just given explanations about the previous budgets. 1 imagine that the OECD studies mentioned by the hon. member were made before these new initiatives were taken by the federal government. We want research and development to be carried out in private industry and this is why we increased tax incentives to help achieve this goal.

subsubtopic: REPORTED DECLINE IN REAL INCOME OF CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my initial question is directed to the Minister of Finance. It arises from the new publication of the Conference Board in Canada entitled "Industrial Relations 1979 Outlook and Issues". This publication came out of a round-table discussion where seven experts passed on our industrial future during this year. At page 2 of the release, referring to the anti-inflation program of the government, it reads:
The program was not effective in controlling prices, but was clearly effective in reducing wage settlements. The experience of declining real income for over a year cannot be expected to induce moderate demands at the bargaining table.
Would the Minister of Finance indicate if he agrees that real incomes on the part of wage earners in Canada fell during 1978?

subsubtopic: REPORTED DECLINE IN REAL INCOME OF CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not have the figures in front of me, but it could be that it was the situation in 1978. If we take the longer view than that, we will realize the net increase in take-home pay by Canadian workers over the last three or four years is above the growth of the gross national product in Canada, and much more than the take-home pay of their colleagues living south of the border.
It is extremely important for the Canadian economy, in order to maintain the competitive position of Canadian businesses and goods, if in 1979 everyone decides to be reasonable and collaborate with the federal and provincial governments to maintain a competitive cost in Canada so that we can take full advantage of the new competitive position of the Canadian industrial sector.

subsubtopic: REPORTED DECLINE IN REAL INCOME OF CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again my question is directed to the Minister of Finance, who indicated that there was a real income drop for wage earners in Canada last year.
As the Conference Board in Canada indicated that the wage settlements in 1979 will have to be in the 8 per cent to 9 per cent range if real incomes are not to continue to be eroded,
Oral Questions
would the minister indicate if he sticks by the guidelines he brought out in February, 1978, dealing with Canada's economic middle-term projections and targets? At that time the minister indicated that average wage settlements in Canada should be 7 per cent, based on prices rising only 5 per cent.

subsubtopic: REPORTED DECLINE IN REAL INCOME OF CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not issued any guidelines this year. We have said that everyone must show restraint, and in negotiations with our own employees we attempted to achieve a good level of settlement, but we want to make sure we are not leading the country into a new period of inflation. That is why I am pleased to report that the public sector, both federal and provincial, by the end of 1978 was two points below the private sector. This is a good change from the situation in 1974-1975, when the public sector was the leader.
Everyone must show restraint. Sometimes circumstances can warrant lower than the federal level, or higher, but I think everyone should keep in mind that we must maintain the competitive position of Canadians in world markets.

subsubtopic: REPORTED DECLINE IN REAL INCOME OF CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. So that we may get a better handle as to where the minister and his government see the Canadian economy evolving, I should like to direct the minister's attention to page 62 of his economic projections in February 1978, at which time he indicated that the share of the gross national product going to wages and salaries would fall during the 1978 to 1981 period, while profits would rise from their 1977 level during that same period.
Will the minister confirm whether it is still the government's position that the wage share of the GNP should fall somewhat, while profits should go up?

subsubtopic: REPORTED DECLINE IN REAL INCOME OF CANADIANS
speechtext:
I think, Mr. Speaker, that in the last four or five years the share of profits in relation to the total Canadian economy has fallen very substantially. I hope that with more profits, those profits will be used for reinvestment so we will improve the capacity of production in Canada, creating more jobs for the workers who are looking for employment.
I do think there is a realization that we need some profits for reinvestment in Canada. For example, a group of workers in my province has settled quite reasonably because they want the pulp and paper industry to reinvest in more modernization and productivity so it will maintain its competitive position. I would like to congratulate that union for taking that responsible stand.

subtopic: STEPS TO ROLL BACK UNFAIR PRICES AND PREVENT FURTHER INFLATION
STEPS TO ROLL BACK UNFAIR PRICES AND PREVENT FURTHER INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for York-Simcoe, I should like to put a question to the Minister of Finance based on the study issued
March 12, 1979

recently by the Conference Board in Canada. However, I am not concerned about a review of statistics or predictions the minister may have made in the past; I am concerned as to what he is going to do now.
In view of the fact that the Conference Board says this is likely to be a tough year in industrial relations because unions are trying to catch up with rising prices, and in spite of the by-play we have had about this sort of thing, will the minister give serious consideration to the finding of ways to roll back unfair price increases so that we can protect the consumer and save this country from another round of inflation?

subtopic: STEPS TO ROLL BACK UNFAIR PRICES AND PREVENT FURTHER INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is possible in an economy like the Canadian economy to control just one small sector. It cannot work this way. We decided in the fall of 1977, when I became Minister of Finance, that we were to get out of controls and put our faith in the market economy, and that is what we are doing at this time. We are trying to make sure that there are no abusers. We have created a commission to look into this problem in order to help the workers of this land.
In the last budget we increased very substantially the tax incentives to those people, through indexation and through other tax cuts, and I do think the take-home pay of Canadian workers has increased regularly over the last few years and they appreciate that, particularly if they compare their situation with the situation in the United States. They want at the same time to make sure that they do not contribute to another round of inflation which could lead us to more controls. If everyone will take his responsibility, we will all be better off.

subtopic: STEPS TO ROLL BACK UNFAIR PRICES AND PREVENT FURTHER INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister made the assertion that the federal government cannot exercise its powers in respect of just one sector of the economy. I would point out to him that the Conference Board in Canada said precisely that the anti-inflation program was effective in holding down wages but did not control prices, so that is the answer to the minister's statement.
May I put the question to the minister again? In view of the fact that the issue facing our economy at this time and throughout this year is unfair price increases, especially in selective areas, will the minister not get serious with this matter, forget his constitutional and his technical problems and find some way to deal with this very real problem that faces the people of Canada?

subtopic: STEPS TO ROLL BACK UNFAIR PRICES AND PREVENT FURTHER INFLATION
speechtext: I am very startled by the assertion of the hon. member that I should not be worried about the constitution of Canada. There are some limitations in the constitution that do not permit the federal government to establish controls unless we are in a crisis situation, and we have to accept that fact.

subtopic: STEPS TO ROLL BACK UNFAIR PRICES AND PREVENT FURTHER INFLATION
speechtext: You did it for wages.

subtopic: STEPS TO ROLL BACK UNFAIR PRICES AND PREVENT FURTHER INFLATION
speechtext:
For the hon. member, with his experience, to say that is very surprising to me, particularly when he suggests that I should not pay attention to the constitution. In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member wants to take the
Oral Questions
Conference Board as his bible, I would point out that the Conference Board predicted last summer that unemployment in Canada this winter would be 9 per cent, and it is only 8.1 per cent; so I would rather not rely on them all the time.

subsubtopic: JOBS LOST THROUGH BANKRUPTCIES-WAGE CLAIMS OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Each year, $4 million in wages and several thousand workers' jobs are lost due to employer bankruptcies, and, some claim, many times more.
Could the minister assure the House that he will try to ensure that employees will continue to have first claim on back wages owed to them, rather than first claims being given to secured creditors such as banks and mortgage companies, or merely establishing a limited fund for employees?

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: JOBS LOST THROUGH BANKRUPTCIES-WAGE CLAIMS OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bankruptcy reform bill was introduced in the Senate last week. It provides that wage earners will rank at the top of preferred creditors with an increase in their preferred claims from $500 to $2,000 for each employee, but they do not rank ahead of secured creditors.
On the other hand, we have provided for a study to determine the feasibility of a funded insurance program which would protect employees of bankrupt companies. That seems to be the best response to that kind of problem.

speechtext:

March 12, 1979

very important aspect of employment strategy as formulated by his department?

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION OF WOMEN IN DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION OF WOMEN IN DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION

I have no reason to believe that the steps announced by the government are not meeting the full support of the Advisory Council.

subsubtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS' ACCESS TO CONFIDENTIAL RECORDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General. I believe he will be aware of reports in the past few days that criminal investigation branch and security service officers have for a number of years had access to the confidential records of the Department of National Health and Welfare. Pursuant to a direction or instruction of July, 1964, these officers may have believed, giving a broad interpretation to that instruction, that that activity had in fact been authorized or condoned by their superiors.

Is that instruction or directive still in force? Is this activity, wherein confidential documents of the Department of National Health and Welfare are available to these law enforcement officers, still being carried out?

subsubtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS' ACCESS TO CONFIDENTIAL RECORDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a matter that has created a great deal of ongoing interest in all members of the House. The hon. gentleman will recall that last year 1 indicated to the House that a directive had issued from the commissioner of the RCMP at my request, so that there was no doubt but that all activities that did not strictly conform to the letter or spirit of any law were to cease. I understand that directive was issued in August, 1978.

subsubtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS' ACCESS TO CONFIDENTIAL RECORDS
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I am not quite sure that the Solicitor General's response would lead me to believe there has been an abrogation of that particular instruction or directive.

Can the Solicitor General tell the House why legislative or regulatory authority has not been sought from him or his predecessors by the various law enforcement agencies? If it has been sought during the past 15 or 20 years, what has been the response of the Solicitor General or his predecessors regarding permission to legalize this rather dubious activity?

subsubtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS' ACCESS TO CONFIDENTIAL RECORDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am not aware of any requests that have been made to any of my predecessors. There were no requests made of me.
I might indicate that the question of the process relating to the investigative instruments that are made available to the RCMP, and how these can be made available to them either by the regulatory process or by the legislative process, is one of the issues that the McDonald commission is charged with deliberating on and making recommendations.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HALIFAX SHIPYARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question to direct to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. It concerns the recent exchanges between the minister and the government of Nova Scotia with respect to the Halifax shipyards.
It is my understanding that the minister has recently expressed great reluctance on the part of the government to move ahead with further aid to the Halifax shipyards. March 12, 1979

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Lessard (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HALIFAX SHIPYARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I expressed these few doubts it is because we are now reviewing the whole Canadian government shipyards assistance program and what I am now considering is an application by a company for development and some modernization. Before making a decision about the file now before us, we want to know precisely what will be the commitments of the provincial government to support development and operations of the seaport and Nova Scotia shipyards, especially in Halifax, because we cannot proceed only on the basis of a commitment by the Canadian government.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HALIFAX SHIPYARDS
speechtext:
A supplementary, Mr. Speaker. What measures has the government taken, or what conversations has the minister had with his colleagues, the Deputy Prime Minister and the president of the super board, with respect to ensuring that Canadian shipyards and, in this case, the Halifax shipyards, have fair access to the six or eight new trawlers that National Sea Products Ltd. are going to build?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that consultations have been held and are even now under way with a view to establishing clearly how to program our undertakings with the shipyards in various cities of Canada. subsubtopic: MR. RAINES-SUGGESTION PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE MISREPRESENTED BY PRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise a matter of privilege concerning an article written by Canadian Press and also a publication put out under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc).
My authority for raising this matter of privilege is as reported in part by Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice Nineteenth Edition. At page 153, under the heading "Misrepresenting Members' Proceedings", it reads as follows:
-misrepresenting their proceedings in parliament, is a breach of the privilege of this House, and destructive of the freedom of parliament.
Also I want to refer to the proceedings of the House of Commons for Monday, March 5, 1979. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) placed a motion under Standing Order 43. I have no quarrel with the reporting in Hansard. The motion as passed read:
[Mr. Chr6tien.J
That this House reaffirms the right of Canadian sealers to go about their legitimate pursuit under the strict supervision of the Government of Canada and the Canadian Federation of Humane Societies, free from harassment and interference.
The motion appeared on page 3795 of Hansard. Further down the page it says:

subsubtopic: MR. RAINES-SUGGESTION PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE MISREPRESENTED BY PRESS
speechtext:
Agreed.
My quarrel arises from a published report the following day in the Ottawa Journal for March 6, 1979, which has just been brought to my attention and which reads:
Meanwhile, in the Commons MPs gave unanimous approval to motion giving full support to the sealers taking part in this year's hunt.
I did not give support to that motion, Mr. Speaker.
Further, there is a publication entitled "Questions and Answers on the Seal Hunt". This publication has also just been brought to my attention. On page 1 of this booklet at the bottom of the page it says:
In March 1977 the Canadian House of Commons unanimously passed a resolution reaffirming the right of Canadians to hunt seals.
Every member of this House of Commons is not in unanimous support of that. Therefore, I feel the proceedings of this House have been misrepresented. I ask that this pamphlet be withdrawn by the Ministry of Fisheries and that that matter be placed on the record.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. RAINES-SUGGESTION PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE MISREPRESENTED BY PRESS
speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also rise on a question of privilege. My question of privilege arises from a response which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) gave me in answer to a question I had put to her. I think her attitude was rather despicable in that she accused me, or seemed to impute motives in my question. She suggested I was here as a lobbyist for the medical profession. In my view, that was a rather cheap shot on her part. It was not up to her to attack my integrity as a member of this House by suggesting that because I am a member of the medical profes-
March 12, 1979

sion 1 am in some way in a conflict of interest situation each time I ask a question in the health field, and particularly when my question relates to the medical profession itself.
It has been a long established practice in this House that medical doctors who are members of parliament are interested in the health field and they ask questions on all aspects of the health care delivery system. If the minister is allowed to get away with this, I do not see how any doctor in this House can get up freely as a member to speak on health issues. If he does imputations will be made in the same way.
To carry this one step further, if a medical doctor cannot speak on health subjects, how can a veteran who is Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald), or how can a farmer who is Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), or how can a lawyer who is Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde), not be accused of being in a conflict of interest situation since they speak in areas in which they either have had direct connections or still do have direct connections? I can also mention the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who is a old age pensioner and frequently raises questions dealing with pensions; yet for some strange reason that seems to be quite all right.
I would say that if the minister is allowed to get away with this imputation of motives we are going to be left with a situation where only members who have no medical background will be allowed to ask questions concerning the health field and those knowledgeable in the health field will not be speaking in this House.
I ask that a ruling be made on this matter. I have been faced with this problem on a number of occasions in the past. As Your Honour will recall, a similar question of privilege was raised on behalf of members of the press gallery.
In my opinion, the minister should withdraw that imputation of motives. With all due respect to you, sir, if she does not 1 would suggest that we take at least a day to review the blues to make sure that this question is properly settled once and for all, so that I will feel free to perform my duties in this place as every other member is entitled to do.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order to question whether these amendments in the name of the minister are in order at this time. The other evening in the committee when we were able to get any information at all out of the minister there was certainly no indication that these amendments would be anything like the amendments which came forward in the committee. This is now the report stage of this bill. I suggest that where amendments change the very intent and meaning of the entire legislation-and I hope to be able to prove that to the Chair very briefly-this is not the time or the place for amendments like that to be entertained by the House.
There are two main purposes for this bill. One is to have a legislative framework to give the government the authority to declare a national emergency with regard to energy supplies,

March 12, 1979
Energy Supplies
distribution and usage in the event of a national emergency which may be completely domestic in origin. The second main purpose is to have a legislative framework in place for the allocation of oil supplies in this country in the event of an international stoppage or an emergency in the oil supplies and petroleum supplies industry.
These two amendments go to the very heart of those two purposes, and in my submission they change very drastically the intent, meaning and administration of the bill which was passed by this Elouse at second reading. There was no hint that these very important amendments were coming either from the minister, the government or any representative of the government in the very prolonged and late hours we put in on Thursday night when the committee dealt with and passed this bill.
The first amendment would give the allocation board set up by the bill the power to study and to keep under review all matters relevant to a full understanding of the international petroleum supply situation. This is directly contrary to what many of us believed, following the word of the minister, in the committee the other evening. The implication was that this board would be run only by part time individuals who would not have very much to do unless the government of the day declared a national emergency or in the event that our responsibilities were triggered under an international agreement.
The first amendment, as I read it, would give the board the responsibility, the function and the duty-whether or not there was a national emergency-to set up facilities and staff to study and keep under review all matters relevant to a full understanding of the international petroleum supply situation and to report from time to time to the minister. That was not the meaning or the intent which was conveyed to the committee the other evening by the minister himself. I cannot quote the actual words the minister used last Thursday evening because as far as I know those proceedings have not yet been printed or published. We simply do not have that information here. However, when questioned about the make-up of the board, the minister indicated that there may be no person involved with the board other than the chairman and that the other six members of the board might not even be appointed. The minister said he wanted it that way so that there would be flexibility.
According to the minister's remarks at second reading and according to his clearly enunciated intention in the committee the other evening, this board really would not come into full force and really would not have very much in the way of duties, staff or budget unless there was a national emergency, and a national emergency would be proclaimed by order in council. Only then would the board's powers and the bill itself be brought into full force and effect. That is in contradiction of the amendment which is being brought forward at this late stage by the minister.
My submission is that the first amendment is very clearly out of order. If the minister wants to withdraw the amendment or if he wants somehow to return the bill to the committee where there could be proper questioning and a proper explana-

tion of the amendment, we would be very happy to oblige. At that time perhaps the matter could be dealt with, although I do not really believe that a government amendment of this magnitude and importance with respect to a bill such as this should be introduced even in the committee. However, we could argue that point in the committee. I think we would all be happy to hear the minister in the committee and to ask him questions in the proper atmosphere and in the informal manner in which that type of interrogation should take place.
My submission is that an amendment which completely changes the administration, the purpose and the intent of a board which was to have full powers of administration only when a national emergency was proclaimed by order in council should not be introduced at the report stage.
The second amendment in the name of the minister is of the same nature. The secondary purpose of this bill is to set up some type of domestic allocation scheme as part of our responsibility under an international agreement Canada signed in 1974, if your Honour can believe it. One of our responsibilities is to have in place a legislative framework so that in the event of an international shortfall in petroleum supplies the government will have in place some domestic allocation scheme under the aegis of the International Energy Agency. Indeed, it was that 1974 agreement which set up the agency and an allocation scheme.

Order, please. This matter has been rather thoroughly argued. There are two or three points I have to consider, one of which I may have to take under advisement for some time, depending on the arguments advanced during the debate. There are some I think I can deal with now.
Report stage proceedings as described in Standing Order 75 are independent of committee proceedings and, therefore, I cannot find motions at the report stage as being out of order simply because they were not previously presented. Report stage is, in fact, independent to a very large degree of the committee stage of a bill. As long as the Standing Orders and the precedents in respect of report stage are adhered to, I am in no position to interfere on a procedural ground simply because a motion may be raised for the first time at the report stage. Therefore, I cannot set this motion aside on this ground.
The second point has to do with the scope of the bill and whether the motion introduces a new concept that goes beyond the original scope of the bill, thereby rendering it out of order. With respect, I think I must conclude, as I mentioned during the course of the argument for the benefit of those wishing to make further contributions, that it is not for the Chair to attempt to decide the full effect of the consideration or the passage of any clause by the House when making an examination of the procedural regularity. Certainly the Chair must be bound by the conditions as they are found, as there may be some complication as a result of the details once an amendment of this sort is passed. I have to address myself only to the general question.
The purpose of the proposed statute is to establish a board for the purpose of dealing with emergency energy supply problems. The purpose of the motion that is before me now seems to be that, in the course of addressing itself to the domestic supply situation, the board shall look into the international aspects of Canada's oil supply. I cannot find that function so different from or unrelated to the function given the board under the statute that I should rule the motion out of order. It seems to me to be an incidental function. It is not for me to decide whether it can or cannot be done or whether it

may lead to complications. 1 have to decide whether that function is sufficiently incidental to the basic function given the board under the main statute that 1 am to consider it a procedurally regular amendment to the bill.
I do so find that it is so related to the function put forward for the board in the bill that this incidental function which is described in the amendment is one to which the Elouse ought to address itself in debate and decide. It was argued that the effect of this amendment was to establish the board now, whereas previously the statute had only the intention of establishing the board in the face of a national emergency. There is one other point which should be raised at this time. When Your Honour is doing some research into the powers and the authority of Petro-Canada itself, could you also take a look at the make-up of the International Energy Agency? This was set up under a 1974 treaty signed by this government and there are now 18 other signatories to that agreement. Basically the administration of the International Energy Agency is carried on at three different levels, as far as representatives of government are concerned. Of course, there is the secretariat which handles the administration, but the three levels of decision-making within that agency, as I understand it, are as follows. I quote from Article 50 of the treaty:
The Governing Board shall be composed of one or more ministers or their delegates from each participating country.
March 12, 1979

As a matter of fact, I believe our own minister is on the governing board, or used to be. Certainly that is a clear indication that the governing board of the International Energy Agency itself has to be composed of people at the ministerial level as far as their being representatives of the countries that are signatory to the agreement is concerned. The next level down is the management committee. In this case I am referring to Article 53, which reads as follows:
The Management Committee shall be composed of one or more senior representatives of the government of each participating country.
Obviously this means that a representative, if not from the ministerial level, should be chosen from at least the top civil servants of the government of each participating country. The third and final level is that of the standing groups. Subsection 1 of Article 54 of the treaty says:
Each Standing Group shall be composed of one or more representatives of the government of each participating country.
I suggest that in actual practice, and in regard to the technical language of the International Energy Agency, the persons who are representatives of governments in respect to the standing groups, where the minister's amendment purports to place a representative of a state-owned oil company, are composed of one or more representatives of the government of each participating country. Under the language that is almost the same for each one of these levels of the agency itself, it is inherent that the representative or representatives of this country on the standing groups of the International Energy Agency should be members of the government, senior civil servants or members of the bureaucracy. By that I mean civil servants and not necessarily public servants.
I suggest to you, sir, that research should be done to decide whether Petro-Canada itself has within its incorporating statute the power to be a representative of the government or whether it is independent of the government. Mr. Speaker, I should like to respond to your invitation to deal with some of these issues. The hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) talked about the structure of the International Energy Agency. He talked about the governing board of the agency. That board deals with a number of matters, not just emergency oil sharing arrangements. In this bill we are concerned with the emergen-
March 12, 1979

cy oil sharing arrangements, not with the research and development aspect or other questions.
Emergency oil sharing arrangements are handled by a senior committee called the standing committee on emergency questions. Attached to that body is an advisory group called the industry advisory board. A number of international companies are associated with this advisory board and Petro-Canada might be associated with this advisory side, the industry advisory board. But there is a second level down. That is the office of the International Energy Agency allocation coordinator. The position of allocation co-ordinator is presently held by the executive director in a dual capacity. His office is concerned with guiding the allocation process. He, too, depends upon advice from the industry, the industry supplies advisory group as it is called. It provides information, it is involved with the co-ordination of the actions of the various companies and it is composed of a selective group of almost exclusively international oil companies. It is advisory, as I say, to the co-ordinator.
The next group down is the International Energy Agency secretariat which is concerned with the implementation of the process. This, too, depends heavily on the international companies. It is concerned with receiving and providing information. It is concerned also with implementing the emergency arrangements through the international companies. As one considers the hierarchy of levels of committees one can see that the international companies play a very important part not just in terms of advice but in terms of implementing the allocation.
We are dealing, then, with international allocation arrangements made by the International Energy Agency. The bill before us is concerned with that process because the agency could trigger the actual proclamation of an emergency situation in Canada as provided in our treaty obligations. Once that happens, the process of allocation will have been determined outside Canada, before the oil gets to Canada, by the International Energy Agency. It will have been determined by the standing group on emergency questions with the advice of international companies. This is why I believe it is essential that we should designate Petro-Canada as a representative of Canada, or as one of the representatives, on this important body.
The question has been asked: Would this in some way go beyond the powers of Petro-Canada itself? I would refer you, Mr. Speaker, to section 3 of the act setting up Petro-Canada. Under the heading "Purposes of the Act" we find the following:
The purpose of this act is to establish within the energy industries of Canada a Crown owned company with authority to explore for hydro-carbon deposits, to negotiate for and acquire petroleum and petroleum products from abroad, to assure a continuity of supply for the needs of Canada ...
I believe Petro-Canada under the International Energy Agency would be doing precisely that-watching and guarding Canadian interests.
Hon. members will recall that it was not long ago that the Exxon Corporation diverted supplies in the order of 25,000 barrels a day of oil destined for Canada from Venezuela
Energy Supplies
through that corporation's subsidiary, Imperial Oil. They were diverted despite the fact that Venezuela had stated it wanted them to go to Canada. An international company acted on that occasion against the wishes of the country of origin, Venezuela, and against the wishes of Canada. It is to protect ourselves against activity of that kind-international companies deciding things for their own purposes, not necessarily for the purposes of the system-that we need a watchdog. That is why we consider Petro-Canada to be so important.
We have witnessed increasing activity on the part of the International Energy Agency and international companies in this regard. Very recently the agency decided it would be important for us collectively to reduce world demand by two million barrels a day, roughly 5 per cent of consumption in the IEA countries, and once again the international agency will be depending upon the international companies. I repeat that this is why it is essential for Petro-Canada to be one of this country's designated participants at the top level of the allocation's process, where the allocation process starts. It starts with the international companies. Such participation is fully consistent with Petro-Canada's own act, as well as with the bill we have in front of us, and I hope a sense of urgency, which has not always been apparent on the other side of the House, will impel us to go forward without delay.

subtopic: REQUESTED ADOPTION OF STANDING ORDERS THAT ENSURE FINANCIAL ACCOUNTABILITY OF GOVERNMENT

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUESTED ADOPTION OF STANDING ORDERS THAT ENSURE FINANCIAL ACCOUNTABILITY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
That this House urges the adoption of Standing Orders which will ensure the government's accountability to the House of Commons for its management of Canada's finances.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I hope I did not give you heart failure as you were in the chair worrying that I might not be here. I certainly intended to be here today to deal with this important subject, one which has plagued parliaments and democratic governments in the free world. The matter to which I refer is the lack of control over public finance which seems to exist. When we consider what has happened in this country, we find that government spending has increased from about $11 billion in 1967 and 1968 to an estimated $53 billion in the next fiscal year. It is more and more difficult to obtain effective democratic supervision over such tremendous amounts of money,
March 12, 1979

and this situation, which is acknowledged everywhere, forces us as parliamentarians to ask some very serious questions about the effectiveness of our control over such spending.
Two important factors must be taken into account when discussing this particular problem. How do we create financial organization within the government itself? That is one question. Second, how can we create more effective methods of scrutiny and control in parliament?
The purpose of this motion is to deal with the latter portion, namely, control mechanisms within parliament itself. I respectfully submit that public expenditures should be presented in a form which will aid members in their critical assessment of public spending. Indeed, that is the reason members of parliament come here in the first place.
Canada is not the only country in the world which has had to face this situation. Let me mention two others as examples which show the directions which have been taken in dealing with this problem. In 1947 the United States Congress formed special budget committees in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. These committees study the President's budget and recommend changes in fiscal policy and spending priorities. The newly created congressional budget office provides technical support to both those committees. I do not have to outline to this House nor, particularly, to the Parliamentary Secretary to President of Treasury Board (Mr. Lefebvre) the difference between Canada and the United States in terms of fora, but it is interesting that this has been done.
Similar efforts to control public spending were established in the British parliament based on the 1969 recommendations of its procedure committee. First of all, in Great Britain the traditional supply estimates are accompanied by an annual white paper which gives parliament specific information on government plans for an immediate three-year period as well as provisional planning for a future period of two years. In other words, parliament has an advance look at the priorities of government in a way which we really do not have in this country. The second aspect is that the old estimates committee has been reorganized to form the newer expenditure committee in the British parliament. That committee is divided into five specialized subcommittees and one general subcommittee. This reconstituted committee takes a much more comprehensive approach to government spending and is better able to assess programs from a long-term policy basis than we are here.
In Canada we have taken some steps as well. In 1969 we established the standing committees of this House as an integral part of the operation of parliament to examine estimates, which are now referred to the standing committees rather than being dealt with in the committee of the whole.
I would be the last to advocate a wholesale return to dealing with estimates in the committee of the whole, although I would be prepared to deal with experiments from the point of view of some estimates from some departments. I know there is some agreement in that regard. Moreover, internally the government introduced the office of Comptroller General for Canada and
Financial Accountability
expanded the resources available to the Auditor General himself. This has also aided the process of budgetary control.
However, with all those steps taken in the last little while- they have been significant steps-there are still strong misgivings in parliament about the ability of the ordinary member of parliament to monitor the financial management and accountability of the government. Parliamentary supervision is one of the cornerstones of our system, and with respect to giving more than lip service in terms of the size of the problem we have not proceeded very far. I suggest that we do not have in the House that kind of control or supervision mechanism that is envisaged by the motion. All the good will in the world will not help us in this task unless we are given the effective tools to utilize in carrying out the task.
In our parliament we need at present more detailed and understandable information on government spending, and that is admitted on all sides of the House. Second, we need a more effective parliamentary committee structure to help us assess the information and make responsible recommendations based on such parliamentary supervision. I use the word "responsible" because I think that gets us out of the field of instinctive reaction, and that reaction of parliament and parliamentarians to this should be based on sure knowledge.
The Auditor General has given a great deal of attention to these points. For example, he underlined in his last report the two main roles of the estimates as follows:
One is to enable parliament to assess the government's proposed allocation of resources and the second is to establish the basics of future accountability by showing why funds are needed, what resources are needed and who is to be accountable.
To improve the financial control, the following modifications are suggested:
-reorganization of the presentation of estimates: a summary volume which shows how resources have been allocated and departmental volumes showing the planned performance of each department.
That was the first suggestion he made and it is a good one. He goes on to say:
-More information in support of statutory appropriations.
Those are the payments that are made and funds which must be gathered to carry out the intentions of the laws passed by parliament.
Such expenses now account for 60 per cent of the budget. We cannot have control without having more information about these expenses.
That is the second recommendation that he made and it is equally sound. Then he went on to say:
-More information on Crown corporations. Parliament should be able to review their yearly activities.
Crown corporations have assumed a larger and larger role in our system. We can debate that role in individual cases, but they are there and parliament should be able to review their yearly activities in a way which we cannot do now. Finally, the Auditor General suggested that:
-Parliament should have the same information as is available to the Treasury Board so that it can responsibly assess departmental programs.

March 12, 1979
Financial Accountability
I say, why not? If Treasury Board has certain information with respect to programs, why should parliament not have that kind of information?
These recommendations made by the Auditor General indicate the present inadequacy of the spending information parliament now receives. The Auditor General also suggests that, in addition to reporting on estimates and public accounts, parliamentary committees should simultaneously be asked to take into account the larger issues of government spending and program development. This is something that our present system does not allow us to do in the way we should do it and in the way the Auditor General felt parliament should have the power to do.
Many points can be made to indicate the problems of the present committee system in ensuring government accountability relating to public spending. These committees are not sufficiently specialized, they are perhaps too large and memberships rotate too often. I think that despite the work of the parliamentary staff and certain other staff, it is fair to say that specialized staff is lacking, the perception of the committee mandate is too narrow and, in the final analysis, the government's attitude towards estimates examination is negative. With respect to further information, I call the attention of the House to the fact that, notwithstanding that there has been a great number of promises, we are still waiting in the dying days of this parliament for a freedom of information act which would be a fundamental tool of parliament which would operate in this milieu.
With these points in mind, I will summarize a suggestion I made in 1976 to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. I consider that it would contribute to parliamentary control of public finance and would put us in a better position to exercise our duty efficiently if we had a standing committee on policy expenditure and programs. Its terms of reference would be to consider the over-all spending priorities of government as well as to consider such estimates as the committee wished to examine on a long-term and extensive basis.
The purpose of this committee would be, in the life of an ordinary parliament, to go in depth into programs of individual departments of government and examine them on a long-term basis so that in a normal four or five year parliament we would be able to go through and examine a number of the important estimates, programs and directions that programs are taking to see whether they are relevant, whether they should be modified, or whether they are meeting the needs for which they were set up. This committee should have available the most complete information about the financial situation of each department and should have access to information which the Treasury Board would have. It would have extensive power, I suggest, with respect to the calling of witnesses. 1 think that this structure would enable parliament to do its job of monitoring the activities of government in a much more effective way.
There is a development occurring now within the government, that of program evaluation. It is in the state of infancy. The Comptroller General of Canada will have a large part to

play in the development of that program. It is something that in terms of the public service is relatively new, and I believe that the internal work with respect to program evaluation could be augmented with respect to the consideration of that work in parliament by a committee structure that would be useful in bringing to parliament those matters which are important to the Auditor General.
I point out to my hon. friend the Parliamentary Secretary to President of Treasury Board that in a phrase from the Speech from the Throne which opened this session of parliament-and I am sure he will remind the House of that in his speech-it is indicated that such a program would be presented to parliament. We are now in the last stage of this parliament and the program has not been presented here. There have been some discussions-I have been part of them and they have been very helpful-but I think that although it is one thing to create this kind of program within the public service to evaluate the programs that are being carried on, the real nub of our program is to have in this parliament a structure by which the work of the evaluation, in terms of the objectives of policy, can be examined by parliamentarians on all sides of the House.
In my respectful submission to the House-and I hope it will be agreeable to members-I suggest that this motion should be passed so that there will be an expression by the House that it is not our desire here to unnecessarily hold up or obstruct the programs of government. It is merely our desire to balance the right of government to proceed with its programs with the right of parliament and the people to make the government accountable to parliament and to the people for the kinds of programs it brings forward. Also it is our desire to engage the attention of members of parliament in looking at the relevancy of programs in a country which is complex and in a society which is pluralistic. The bottom line of the operation of a democratic government is the accountability of that government. That is the purpose of this motion, and 1 hope it commends itself to the House.

subtopic: REQUESTED ADOPTION OF STANDING ORDERS THAT ENSURE FINANCIAL ACCOUNTABILITY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a very interesting motion which has been brought forth this afternoon by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker). I for one welcome the opportunity to speak on it. 1 would like to take this time to remind all hon. members of a number of significant changes and initiatives taken by the government to demonstrate its concern with establishing an appropriate accountability framework in the management of government programs.
One of these initiatives was the establishment of the royal commission on financial management and accountability on November 22, 1976. The chairman of this commission, Mr. Allen T. Lambert, said the following:
One of the overriding objectives of the final report which the commission plans to submit... is to establish within the government a workable framework of accountability and control for individual departments and agencies in the management of their affairs, and to strengthen the system of accountability by the government to parliament.
The formation of the royal commission was an acknowledgement by the government that with the growing size and complexity of government today, not only in Canada but in all progressive democratic countries, there is a need to re-examine the means of accountability by the government to parliament.
The commission focused its attention on three main subjects: the role of cabinet and central agencies such as the Treasury Board secretariat and Privy Council Office in establishing priorities, allocating resources and maintaining broad control over individual departments and agencies; the role of the deputy head and the management of departments, and the system of accountability to the minister, the executive, the central organizations and parliament; and the system of direction, control and accountability of Crown agencies.
In the interim report of the royal commission published in November, 1977 some interesting questions were posed. For example, in the present day context can the minister alone continue to be held accountable to parliament for every aspect of the administrative performance of the department or Crown agency? This challenges the fundamental doctrine of ministerial responsibility. What information is necessary to enable parliament to carry out its role as protector of the public purse? Could the performance of parliamentary committees involved in the surveillance of government spending be made more effective? Should there be other means for conducting parliamentary review of the performance of departments and Crown agencies, apart from the consideration of the estimates and the public accounts?
Financial Accountability
The progress report of the royal commission directed its attention to the elusive meaning of the word "accountability". It indicated how it could be effective when the commission reported the following:
In its simplest terms, to be accountable means to be liable to be called to account for an accepted responsibility, but this definition is not practical unless it is extended to include a judgment upon the performance of that responsibility. Thus, meaningful accountability requires that there be:
-procedures for setting objectives and goals and assigning responsibility to
achieve results;
-a reporting system or systems that provide information on the progress
made toward the achievement of goals;
-a review of the reported results with the purpose of evaluating performance.
In effect, the commission suggested that there are two accountability frameworks which underpin democratic and responsible government. It indicated:
These are the way in which parliament holds the executive to account for the conduct of its administration of government and the way in which the executive in turn holds the senior managers of the public service and Crown agencies to account for their administration.
The government recognized the dual framework, and that is why it has continued to meet the challenge on two fronts: improving the management ability of public servants, and providing better disclosure of the spending plans and program results through the estimates and public accounts. Furthermore, major improvements in the parliamentary process have been made through such bodies as the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates and special committees to examine specific matters.
Another initiative taken by the government to demonstrate its concern with accountability was its examination of direction, control and accountability of Crown corporations. As You Honour is aware, a blue paper was produced on this subject in 1977. The paper examined such difficult questions as to what extent Crown corporations should be used as instruments of public policy when the pursuit of policy objectives may detract from the financial performance of such corporations. Also it examined how increased responsiveness to public policy can be reconciled with the arm's length relationship which in theory a public enterprise requires government ministers and parliament to maintain with Crown corporations. The paper was published to encourage public discussion and comment prior to the introduction of a Crown corporations bill in parliament.
On the general subject of accountability I should like to draw Your Honour's attention to the new Auditor General Act passed by the House of Commons on June 29, 1977, and subsequently passed without amendment by the Senate. A key change in the scope of the responsibilities of the Auditor General is contained in section 7(2) of the act. It reads as follows:
Each report of the Auditor General.. . shall call attention to anything that he considers to be of significance and of a nature that should be brought to the attention of the House of Commons, including any cases in which he has observed that. .. money has been expended without due regard to economy or efficiency; or satisfactory procedures have not been established to measure and report the effectiveness of programs, where such procedures could appropriately and reasonably by implemented.

March 12, 1979
Financial Accountability
As all hon. members are aware from reading the Auditor General's report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1978, in exercising his new mandate the Auditor General has focused on procedures in cost effectiveness and value for money. Also his report contained suggested models for improving the information display of departmental estimates. These models will be taken into account in the joint Treasury Board/Comptroller General study of the form of the estimates which now is under way. Extensive discussions have taken place on this subject with the public accounts committee and with witnesses from the Treasury Board secretariat, the Comptroller General's office and the office of the Auditor General.
The government is continuously searching for improvements. It has established its own internal monitoring function to ensure that there will be sound management and control within the over-all government accountability framework. I am speaking, of course, of the establishment of the office of the Comptroller General and the appointment of Mr. Harry Rogers as Comptroller General. Mr. Rogers' appointment was announced in February of last year by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and he began his new duties on April 2, one year ago.
