subtopic: REQUESTED ADOPTION OF STANDING ORDERS THAT ENSURE FINANCIAL ACCOUNTABILITY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Yes, supported by all parties. The Comptroller General's responsibilities include financial administration policy as it affects departments and agencies of the government, the form of the accounts of Canada, the form and the content of the government's financial statements, including those of its departments and agencies. His responsibilities include also the methods and procedures of control that are followed by departments and agencies, including budgetary methods and budgetary control systems, functional responsibilities for financial organizations, departments and agencies, the professional development of financial officers, and all related areas of financial management and control.
In addition, the Comptroller General has two other major responsibilities in improving management and control, namely, performance measurements and program evaluation. It is through these two major tools that accountability can be explicitly stated. The Treasury Board policy on performance measurement was issued in 1976, and its policy on program eveluation followed in 1977.
The government recognizes in the face of a long-term period of restraint that major new policy decisions and programs will need to be financed out of existing programs. Organizational skills must shift from planning and implementing to managing and controlling. In this connection, the federal government has endorsed three key management objectives: first, improving economy in the acquisition of assets; second, improving efficiency in their use and in the administration of program expenditures; and third, improving the effectiveness of government programs in achieving their objectives. These objectives complement the objectives of maintaining high standards of

financial prudence and probity in the conduct of the government's financial affairs.
In addition to the work of the Comptroller General in bringing about needed improvements, a series of seminars has been given to enable deputy ministers and other senior officials to gain a better appreciation of the financial management process. The emphasis of the seminars is on senior officers' responsibilities in this important domain.
Therefore, it will be clear to this House that there is already a climate of good will both in the government and in the public service to continue our best efforts in establishing the most appropriate system of accountability in the management of this government's financial affairs.
Before closing, I should like to underline and once again bring to the attention of hon. members of this House the work now going on in the public accounts committee. For the past several weeks, with meetings and briefings, many times a week, this committee is and has been gathering ideas and suggestions from its members, with constant assistance from the Auditor General and his highly qualified staff, the Treasury Board secretariat represented by Mr. Larry O'Toole, and the Comptroller General of Canada, in order to put together what we of the committee feel will be a very important report to this House on what we believe should be included in the future form of the estimates.
The Auditor General has mentioned more than once that this working group, as he refers to it, is a fantastic breakthrough and a major step forward toward financial accountability and control. This study by the public accounts committee has been an example of co-operation by members of parliament from the official opposition-one of its members chairs the committee-and members from the government side, as well as from Treasury Board, the office of the Comptroller General and the Auditor General. Members hope that some of their recommendations will be evident in the estimates to be tabled next year and each year following until an almost new form of estimates is published, in order that they may become more comprehensive and useful to everyone concerned.
I feel confident that enough data is on the record of this committee's proceedings to ensure that there will definitely be a continual change for the better in the estimates, and when I say "better", I mean better for the parliament of Canada, the public of Canada, the public service and, of course, the Government of Canada.
The committee has not been able to arrive at a final consensus yet, especially on how the estimates should be handled by the House and its committees. It may be that this subject will be part of a study by the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. I am sure I speak for all hon. members of the committee when I say that it has done a great many weeks of very intensive and hard work. I am sure the evidence of this work will be seen in the form of the estimates. If the committee can accomplish its work I hope that a report can be tabled in this House at this stage which will indicate what that committee has accomplished.
March 12, 1979

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) for bringing this motion on today, particularly as he is the House leader of the Conservative party and may have some role to play in the next government. If that is the case I look forward to holding him to fulfilling some of the recommendations he has made.
I think it is safe to say that, as far as members of parliament are concerned, expenditures of government are totally beyond control in any way, shape or form. I listened with great interest when the parliamentary secretary indicated what the government intends to do. The government is always going to do something and it always has done something. It has carried out a great many studies and it has always had a great deal of input from civil service and other interested individuals and groups; but the situation has continually worsened.
When I first came here total government expenditures amounted to about $10 billion or $15 billion. I doubt if they were much higher than that. Today total expenditures have increased to $52 billion. Since the beginning of this parliament expenditures have more than doubled, having jumped from $23 billion to $52 billion. We were not able to handle expenditures very well when they amounted in total to $10 billion or $15 billion, and today we cannot handle them at all.
It must shock new members, as it must shock any thinking Canadian, that we are coming to the end of the month when we will pass those expenditures amounting to $52 billion without knowing what 90 per cent of the expenditures are, let alone whether they are needed. It is all right for us to say that the Auditor General is able to look into them on our behalf. I congratulate the auditor generals we have had for the work they have done. They have found horses on the payroll and a number of other major sensational abuses. I think there are about ten or 12 such sensational abuses each year. I would ask what members of parliament have been able to do about these abuses, the ten or 12 sensational ones that hit the headlines each year. I suggest they have been able to do absolutely nothing.
I suggest there is absolutely no machinery in place by which members of parliament can do anything about such abuses. We have a Comptroller General who may keep a few civil servants honest, and who may have been able in some way to control the manner in which some expenditures are made.
When listening to the parliamentary secretary a few minutes ago I was interested to hear him say the government is going to promote efficiencies and general control over the expenditures of the Treasury Board and the BED ministers. This government has decentralized, that is what it has done. For instance, it took the Department of Veterans Affairs to that minister's riding in Prince Edward Island, about as far away from the government as you can get. If this government stays in office for another five years we will probably have to go through another country to get there.
Financial Accountability
What have we done about buying pencils, for example? I often wonder what the Comptroller General and the BED ministers think about this if it is not in their ridings-we are buying pencils in Matane, for instance. The Department of Supply and Services increased its purchases tenfold in that area. That is not what I understand as efficiency. To be efficient you buy in bulk; you do not make purchases in every minister's riding. Can we control that sort of thing in the estimates? Are we in a position to do anything about those matters? The patronage exercised by this government is rampant. We do not know the levels where it exists. Patronage certainly is not efficiency. It is where somebody who cannot be elected to government or somebody who is related to someone who cannot be elected, is put in a responsible position where they do irresponsible things. That is surely not an economy.
One of the reasons I hope there is a change in government is that something might be done about some of these problems and not just more committees set up. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) says we do not want to go back to the days of committee of the whole. I think we could gain something by going back to that. We might have to limit the time or, as they do in other countries, set three months aside for it.

speechtext:
I do not see what I have to withdraw. I am giving the hon. member full credit for having done this. Let me give an example. I have heard him many times on the question

March 12, 1979
Financial Accountability
of veterans affairs, and when he won a point after considerable effort I thought it was a good reward for his people. I am sure he did not do it for other reasons. I hope hon. members will agree that I did not do it for other than a good reward on behalf of my constituents.
I sympathize with the member who interjected. He has not been here long enough to remember when we really had some control over estimates. When we had control over estimates, using the time factor, many amendments were made. How many members can say today that they are able to change anything in the estimates when they are brought before parliament by civil servants? The government does not really understand what is going on. In many cases I am sure the estimates make provision for civil servants operating in concerns of branches of departments that the government does not know exist, and which are self-perpetuating.
It is not going to be easy to supervise the expenditures of parliament. It is not easy in other countries either. It is not easy to control statutory expenditures. We pass a piece of legislation and in perpetuity provide gratuities to agencies that are never questioned. I am sure that if some of them kept very quiet and did not rock the boat, did not start muck-raking or department building, they would find themselves in no difficulty unless they asked for additional statutory expenditure. I am sure the same thing is true of Crown corporations. We really never supervise them. I agree with the parliamentary secretary who says that we probably have to keep at arm's length from them because, if we do not, they would only be departments of government. But we must examine their costs and the direction they are taking.
The charge has often been made that a Crown corporation cannot use money efficiently. The Canadian National Railways is a good example. It is a wonderful organization now because it is making money. The thing is, it always made money but we charged so much of the debt to it that was incurred 50 or 100 years ago that the interest was never paid off, let alone the debt. Now that the debt has been written off we are no longer in the difficulty.
The Canadian Pacific Railway was the only beneficiary of that bad accounting system. When we could show that CN was in debt we could always work out the railroad tariff on the basis that it was not making any money and, because of that, CPR got the benefit of all the subsidization that had to go into making the CN a viable operation.
Recently in the news, Canadian Pacific was screaming about the fact that Air Canada, a Crown corporation, was cutting air fares to a degree that would bankrupt Canadian Pacific Air as they do not have the lucrative lines Air Canada has. Several years ago Air Canada was only a stepchild of the Canadian National Railways and their debt structure was tied to it. Now that we have established Air Canada independently it is a very successful corporation. Maybe most of our Crown corporations would be financially sound if we set up the right kind of structure for proper accounting so that members of parliament would know whether they were operating efficient-

ly and serving a need. The machinery is now in place for us to examine that.
I am not sympathetic with the way the government has handled this problem. All it has done in the last eight or ten years is create more Crown corporations, and establish more controls and committees. It has a committee or royal commission or something to handle every problem that parliament should face itself. If we faced them we would at least know what we are trying to accomplish, rather than establishing all these backroom controls, with the proliferation of civil servants, patronage, and decentralization. Decentralization only seems to satisfy those ministers whose areas are affected.
In my opinion, this government is not efficient. It is not prepared to provide members of parliament with information on which to base reasonable decisions. How many members really understand why the government is able to take money out of the treasury, or borrow at a rate of 12 or 13 per cent in order to stabilize the Canadian dollar? When the Conservatives tried to do that with huge expenditures they were able to stabilize it within about two cents of what it would normally have been. And yet we are allowing the government to make those huge expenditures in the billions of dollars. This is money borrowed which we will probably never be able to pay off in our lifetime. This will saddle our children and their children with a debt for absolutely no purpose.
If the government really wants to do something about stabilizing the dollar, why not peg it? This dirty float is a totally dishonest way of calculating expenditures because there is no statutory control. There is certainly no way in which members of parliament can do anything, except through the public accounts committee. This committee looks at bad debts after they are incurred and wonders how in hell we got them and for what. It has nothing to do with controlling expenditures. In addition, it does not teach us very much because civil servants have a new word for control. The next time they try something else again.
We have set up all kinds of commissions to decide how to make the expenditures of the nation more controllable. In the final analysis we do not need to delegate control over the expenditures of our nation. That is the responsibility of elected members of parliament. This should be exercised in the House of Commons and it should be carried out on the basis of every bit of the information the government has used in making its decisions. If the government makes bad decisions, if it makes them on the basis of poor information, and says that it had done the best possible, members of parliament should be able to look at the information that is available and decide whether the expenditure is justified and whether the information being provided is sufficient. Then they should be able to do something about it.
This government has abused its majority. It has abused its majority every time it has had one. The only time we have had good government in Canada since I have been a member of parliament is when we had a minority government. Why, Mr. March 12, 1979

Speaker? Because in the final analysis all members of parliament look at the problems for themselves, decide whether there is a good or bad solution, and vote accordingly. Each member looks at the question and makes a decision. With a majority government, all they do is stand up and say, "Are you ready to receive my assistance for the next election, and God willing, 1 will be elected." They have decided nothing on their own. The decision is made as a block because they have a majority in parliament. No one can stand up and say they are honestly interested in allowing parliament to control expenditures.
I would like to mention the blue book. When I first came here one could look in the blue book, which contains the estimates of the expenditures for the forthcoming year. This book is not much thicker now, but it has certainly become a lot less useful. What is written in under the headings of each department? It is propaganda. It describes what the government proposes to do in that department and what it hopes to accomplish. Who cares? We are supposed to be looking at the expenditures in the departments and deciding if we think they will be able to do whatever they want to accomplish. We bloody well can't do that with the estimates we have.
At one time there was a list of all these high-falutin' people who got more than $20,000. Now the ones getting more than $50,000 are not listed nor are the ones getting more than $75,000. No matter how high the salary goes these people are not listed any more. At one time we were able to look at this list.
When I used to look through these lists the high-paid ones were usually alcoholics or something else. These were people who were stuck into a corner in a department where they did not have to do anything.
1 made a complaint about something that happened in a department. I was told not to go to the director because he had a bunch of toy trains in his desk and all he did was play with toy trains. I am sure many members here know who that is. There was another one we referred to; we found out that his secretary put him back in his chair 37 times in one month.
At one time we were able to phone a department for information. There was none of this "b.s." that you get from Manpower today. The five top people in these departments, without exception, are at meetings every day. It is not possible to get those people unless someone is conscientious and stays after four o'clock because the rest of the time they are at meetings. There are even meetings that last all day. We know this goes on, and when we look at the book and cannot find out who the director is or get information on expenditures, it is very sad. The only thing that is brought up to date is the telephone book, and that is changed every four months. That is probably not more than eight months out of whack.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us urges the adoption of Standing Orders which will ensure the government's accountability to the House of Commons for its management of Canada's finances.
The entire thrust of the motion is in terms of the rules and procedures of this House on the assumption that if we behave in a different way or follow a different or modified set of Standing Orders we can achieve that great goal of accountability to which all parliamentarians aspire.
The Auditor General, and the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Lefebvre), have pointed out very well, that there cannot be any accountability unless we resolve the very basic problem with the kind of information we are going to have. I suggest that while there is a structural problem, members of this House who are really concerned about accountability take on a chore, and it is a chore, of attending the Public Accounts Committee and reading the documents. The documents are lengthy and they are not always easily understood. The people who are working with the Auditor General are attempting to provide parliament with the tools parliament needs if it is ever to manage properly the funds it votes.
The government has supported the Auditor General and given him the necessary resources. By his own admission there has never been a question or any shortcoming in terms of his budget or the specialized manpower required to do a job to the extent to which it was required. I believe there has never been a more qualified group of management consultants and technical experts assembled in Canada than has been assembled by the present Auditor General in an honest effort to come to grips with some very fundamental problems.
Basically with regard to every government department there are three sets of documents which have to be examined. There are estimates on the basis of which parliament votes supply. This is the mechanism by which the resources for the fiscal period anticipated are described and allocated. There are the public accounts which are the story of what has happened, the story of how the money was spent. In nearly every case there is a departmental report, frequently in narrative form, with appendices at the end, from the estimates or from the public accounts. But the Auditor General has documented chapter and verse of cases where one cannot go from one to another in a logical and consistent way. The form, breakdown and content are really quite incomprehensible in the way in which they are placed before us as parliamentarians and the nation at large.

As the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) indicated, he has pointed out the deficiencies in the consistency of treatment of the estimates. If you cannot go back and forth from one to the other, you are lost before you start. The

Financial Accountability
Auditor General pointed out that matters relating to statutory votes are frequently not even in the estimates. They are not even provided. Something like $20 billion of that $50 billion is statutory.
He pointed out again that when he examined the Crown corporations in great detail, he found a great difference in range. Some Crown corporations were doing a good job of setting out their accounts in a form which was understandable, but a large number were not.
We are now having Treasury Board undertake a major revision of the Financial Administration Act and the schedules by which the Crown corporations are to be classified. We have been given illustrated models of the way in which it would have been possible for the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority to present its estimates. This would have been in a form that is comprehensible, one which would have permitted parliament to make a rational examination of the priorities assigned to that Crown corporation, how its plans related to what had been done the previous two years, and what is anticipated two years ahead.
Those of us who had the opportunity of looking at what might have been the way in which the information was presented were struck by what we saw and heard. It is quite clear that this is the direction in which we must go. The question of how the estimates are to be prepared in a form by which parliament can properly use them is a very fundamental question. Traditionally, the estimates have been the tool of Treasury Board, and one branch of Treasury Board by which they allocated resources.
In a recent period of restraint, cabinet ministers were called in and told to chop $100 million here, $200 million there, and that they must stay within these over-all limits. The estimates were looked upon by Treasury Board in a proprietary way.
When Treasury Board was told by the Auditor General that the form of the estimates may have been good enough for resource allocation but was not good enough for accountability to parliament, the Public Accounts Committee had to break ground. It was very interesting to see. I regret that the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) is not here. For his work as chairman of the Public Accounts Committee, I want to pay him tribute in this place. I believe he has done a good job.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my final speech on third reading I wish to direct attention to certain matters which have been neglected in the course of our deliberations, or which have not been emphasized with sufficient force.
The announcement the minister made last May has had a disastrous affect not only upon the co-operative housing program but upon the neighbourhood improvement program as well as upon projects envisaged by cities, towns, and municipalities across the country. Great uncertainty was created by that announcement. The minister admitted that the central government would be backing away from previous commitments and policies.
It is worth recalling that in 1968 the then minister of housing, Mr. Hellyer, was supposed to devise a new housing and urban policy for Canada. That urban policy and that housing policy involved the federal government. It took him some time, and he switched parties before anything was done, but the thrust of that policy was that the federal government had a role to play in the solution of the urban problems of Canadians. It had a role to play in planning and the assembly of land in order to prevent speculation. It had a role to play in the designation of certain areas in the cores of our cities- improvement areas-in order to get at the problems of poverty and the physical decline of the centres of our cities as well as lack of opportunity for many of our people. That was the thrust and direction of the policy, which was expanded during the minority government of 1972 to 1974.
March 12, 1979

With the co-operation of the New Democratic Party the Liberal party at that time was prepared to bring in income supplements for many Canadians. It was prepared to bring in programs to provide funding for some co-operative housing, and it recognized for the first time the principle of non-profit ownership in the development of our housing policy. If those were the days of the new liberalism, we are now in the final dying days-and I say this despite the defection of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart)-of the new conservatism.
If the hon. member for Cochrane sees the Liberal party as moving to the left, the only conclusion there can be is that he is suffering from political dyslexia because what I see is precisely the opposite movement. I see a movement to the right. The federal government is saying to the cities that it cannot get involved any more. It is saying to our co-operative institutions that it is not prepared to fund them any longer. It is saying to urban Canadians that if they have problems they will have to direct them to the provincial governments. This is the standard of leadership we can now expect from the Liberal government.
This motley collection of amendments which we have attempted to improve, and which to some extent we have succeeded in improving, is the end result of this policy, this hodge-podge, this attempt at some kind of appeasement of what the Liberal party sees as a conservative mood amongst the voters of Canada.
What does this bill do? It amounts to a full-fledged retreat by the federal government from the solution of our housing and urban development problems. It amounts to a full-fledged retreat, and when the time comes to look at the role of the federal government, I hope the voters of Canada will see that the federal government has put its toes in the water, with respect to trying to solve some of our problems, quickly decided to pull its feet back and daintily returned to the comfortable beaches of the new conservatism. That is precisely the direction in which this government is headed. It is headed, not toward the political left as my colleague, the hon. member for Cochrane, stated last week, but toward the political right.
These amendments are the direct result of a shift on the part of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). Now we have the government becoming a banker. It is not the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation any more. It is the central insurance and banking corporation because the federal government will no longer be directly involved in housing. The government has said it will not get involved, that it will leave housing up to the private sector and that it will assume that trust companies, lending companies and banks will play the role, in terms of innovative social policy, the government was supposed to start playing from 1972 to 1974. We on this side know that that is not exactly what is going to happen, and the time will come once again-I foresee it readily-when whatever party forms the government of this country it will have to recognize that the urban and housing needs of Canadians will have to be met directly by means of
Housing
government intervention. That intervention will come at the federal level as well as the provincial level. Both levels will have to work co-operatively, recognizing that they both have roles to play in meeting the social needs of their citizens. We know that will happen again because a need will have to be met, and that need simply has not been met by the policies of the current government.
The new Jerusalem was announced by the minister in May. Unfortunately, it took eight or nine months before the legislation was brought before the House, so the governments of the cities and towns of this country, the real governments for most of our citizens, the governments to which they look first, did not know where to turn. That is the housing crisis the minister has not recognized. It is a crisis created by the minister's own inability and the cabinet's own inability to decide what to do.
Today the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) talked about the benefit of his policy of encouraging no-name products in the consumer field. We have no-name products for cabinet ministers today because the average Canadian does not know who is in the cabinet. Cabinet ministers cannot make up their minds about what social policies to bring before the people of Canada. The crisis created by this government is such that communities and municipalities are crying out for federal government policies. They are crying out for money to build recreational facilities, to build sewage facilities, and to deal with the urgent problems they face because they do not have capital to deal with construction problems.
The minister forced us into agreeing to put these amendments through quickly, but a condition was that he recognize that we also had amendments and ideas to be considered. What we got was not the best, because we would have much preferred to be able to bring before the committee of this House which deals with housing, representatives of the Canadian Council on Social Development, the Canadian Welfare Council, national poverty organizations, provincial organizations, co-operative housing organizations, and the private lending institutions which are going to fill the gap. I would like to have heard precisely what plans they had for replacing the vacuum which has been created by the policies the Liberal party adopted from the Conservative party. Instead, we were forced into a position where we had to accept in the committee of the whole at very short notice a series of amendments which three parties in this House agreed would be necessary to get the kind of consent required to get the measures through quickly.
If we look at the level of funding which is being provided, the bottom line, the dollars and cents which are going into these programs-the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program and the Community Services Grants Program-the level of funding is down. This government is masquerading a series of amendments as being progressive and as amounting to a positive policy, when what they amount to are an excuse for cutbacks. The minister knows this. Mr. Hession certainly knows it because he has written to the minister about it. The minister said that RRAP is going to be made universal. Well,

March 12, 1979
Housing
264 times nothing is still nothing, and that is what we have been left with, 264 ridings with practically no money for residential rehabilitation.
The Community Services Grants Program replaces ten programs with three, and that means that the level of funding will not be adequate. As I said many times in the committee, we will not get the funding which is needed for community development or for recreational facilities, and all the money which goes to the provinces will be used for the hardware of urban development.
I am not saying that hardware is not important; it is vital. People need to have the kind of sewage treatment which is fundamental to healthy living. I recognize that, and my party recognizes it. But we do not accept what the minister is saying when he says that all our urban needs will now be satisfied by the money which is being provided to the provinces, when we know that the level of funding under community service grants is far lower than it was under all the old programs under which the cities, towns and municipalities would go to the federal and provincial governments and attempt as best they could to barter their future needs. So we reject the approach of the Liberal government, we reject the cutbacks, we reject the $350 million diminution in the CMHC. You can call it the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or you can all it anything you wish, you can masquerade it, tart it up any way you want, but it amounts to the same old charade, and that is more grandiose programs with less money to fund them, which means that the urban needs of our communities will not be met.
I say to you tonight, Mr. Speaker, that the way in which the government has presented these programs has been irresponsible. Ministers have put themselves in a position where they have had to force the House to consider these proposals hastily because they have created a need in the municipalities which was not there until they cut off their program and until they engaged in this so-called avenue of cutbacks and decreased the expenditure as a result of the miraculous conversion which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has suffered following his trip to Bonn in the summer of 1978. We in our party have attempted to bring forward amendments which would have a constructive effect. We have attempted to say: Let us put a damper on this lemming-like rush toward cutbacks and let us try to provide something for our cities, let us give them the leeway to assemble land and to provide affordable housing, let alone the non-profit motive to work; let us put the co-operative motive to work.
Well, it is an odd assembly of events that has brought us here tonight. We have a housing crisis in Canada and we have the government's amendments, and the two have absolutely nothing to do with each other. The government's amendments are brought about as a result of its determination to cut back on government spending, nothing more or less than that, and the housing crisis in Canada is created today by the fact that we have had an inflation in housing prices which has gone on

for the past ten years and with which the government has been incapable of dealing, and we have an inflation in the cost of money which the government has deliberately created by government policy.
We say it is high time the people of Canada were given the opportunity in a free election to decide what they want to do about that crisis. Do they want to adopt the policy of the government which is to let things ride as they are, in the hope that the best will work out and for the Minister of Public Works and Minister of State for Urban Affairs to present a striptease to the Canadian public saying, "If you are good boys and girls, maybe in two or three years we will give you a tax credit"? Is that what the people of Canada want? No. On the other hand, we can take the policies of the Conservative party-

That is not so, Mr. Speaker. You are sacrificing the present demands of the Canadian public for a tax cut on the altar of some future event which may or may not take place, that is, the buying of a house. We on this side of the House say that if you want to deal with the problem of the cost of money, you should deal with it directly instead of pussyfooting around the side of the problem and trying to make it palatable. You do not make high interest rates palatable; you get the high interest rates down. And if you want to deal with the cost of land, you start controlling the cost of land by getting at speculation which has more than doubled the cost of land in surburban areas of our major centres in the past five years, which has meant that many Canadians have become millionaires as a result of a pure hazard, that hazard being whether or not they happen to own acres of land.
We in our party say: provide tax relief but provide it for all Canadians, do not make it selective and do not make it depend on whether or not you own a house. There are senior citizens in apartments and there are senior citizens in homes. They both deserve a tax break. Do not be discriminatory and prejudicial; deal with all the people of Canada fairly. We say: if you want to get at the cost of money, do it directly; do not pussyfoot around the side of the problem. If you want to deal with the cost of land, deal with it directly; do not pussyfoot around the edge of the problem; get at the root of the problem, which is speculation and monopoly conditions in the ownership of land. Those are the problems that you face in the country. They have nothing to do with the amendments brought forward by the minister with respect to these problems.
March 12, 1979

There will be many opportunities in the coming months for us to discuss, on various platforms and in various ways, the programs of our party. I have said many times before in the House, particularly in this debate, that the people of Canada will decide who has the right approach, who are talking out of both sides of their mouths, and who is promising the world and delivering nothing. But it is important to recognize-I have said this before-that promising benefits to Canadians will not make it easier for a single Canadian to buy a house. Buying votes or renting votes, as seems to be the propensity of the Liberal government, promising something and taking it away six months later, will not buy a single vote and will not buy a single home, and it is time the people recognized it.
This bill does not deal with the housing crisis, nor is it intended to deal with it. The fact that it and the housing crisis have come up at the same time is simply the result of the government's inactivity and incompetence.
We have attempted to improve the bill as a result of our amendments in committee, and 1 pay respect to the minister of State for Urban Affairs and to my colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott), for having taken the time to try to work constructively with me and with representatives of other parties in an attempt to get a better bill. We have a better bill now than we had before, but I suggest it would not be very difficult.
The housing problems of Canadians are serious, and the affordability problems are serious because there are far too many Canadians who cannot afford to buy a house and there are far too many Canadians who are paying too much for their shelter needs. These needs will not disappear, and this bill will do absolutely nothing to solve the problems. That is the approach that I have taken to this legislation from the time it was announced in November and December to the time we discussed it on second reading, to the time we went through it in committee, and now, and that will be the approach we will be taking in the months to come.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend my colleagues in the House for the excellence of this debate. I believe that some very constructive things have been offered, and I am sure the minister is paying rapt attention to them.
Areas of poor housing are a reality, as are unemployment and poverty, unchallenged workers and under-educated people and poor living conditions. Disillusioned youth and senior citizens waiting out their golden years in idleness are realities too. The awareness of these injustices and the determination to end them are also realities. With wisdom, courage and determination we can overcome these difficulties, or we can hide our heads in the sand, talk about programs which we know will not be funded adequately, and leave ghettos of frustration, worry and neglect, areas of disillusion and disenchantment, and future problems of tremendous magnitude in terms of hatred and bitterness.
Housing
The Athenians taught us that greatness is not related to size. Large cities have taught us that ghettos within and strip development without are enemies of the quality of life, and that we must focus the attention of all levels of government on the very important concept of involving citizens in the future design and composition of the communities in which they will live, work, and have their being. If a city is just to be banks, stores, finance companies, schools, parks and cinemas; if it is just to be houses, cement, streets and roads, then we have betrayed the trust of thousands of people who have worked to make our cities a place where people can live in dignity, security and harmony, and where the great achievements of civilization, culture, hopes and dreams for our fellow citizens should be available to all. If these are to be the goals and objectives of this parliament, we will need all the programs which are possible under the bill before us, and many more. We shall have to identify successes in other areas and focus our purchasing power into realistic programs in the field of housing.
I do not know how many wealthy people have large mortgages and pay high interest rates on them. Some government spokesmen seem to know a lot of these people, but I know very few. I do know a lot of people in the lower and middle income groups who have large mortgages, and pay high interest rates and high property taxes. I know the ability to deduct interest payments and property taxes from their income tax would make life a little more like living and would enable them to take their place in the community with greater security. Also I know that it would open up the opportunity and privilege. Imaginative programs like this one and constructive suggestions should not be overlooked simply because they come from the other fellow. Most certainly they should not be the subject of windjamming rhetoric by small-minded politicians and their political hacks.
The country needs the outpouring of imagination, ingenuity and hard work, not just to provide houses but to provide homes for people. We must encourage human dialogue, common experiences, purposes, understanding and respect, which tie Canadians together. Our municipalities must be encouraged to pay greater attention to neighbourhoods, civic pride and the feeling of community.
The sense of community and belonging enhances the feeling of security and a sense of one's own worth in the over-all championship of others. This is the feeling most of us share as Canadians in our Canadian experience. But it is a feeling shared to a far lesser degree by thousands of Canadians who are denied the opportunity of owning their own homes, and by others who suffer daily the ravages of poverty in inadequate housing situations. 1 hope the minister, in the course of his remarks, will assist me by indicating where in the legislation we can find the magnitude of thrust which is essential to meet this challenge.
The complexity of administering a nation or a great city is very much a deterrent to providing the quality of life essential to the feeling of community in our larger municipalities.

March 12, 1979
Housing
Members of parliament representing large urban ridings will agree they know very few of their constituents on a first name basis, and that only a very small proportion of their constituents know each other or talk to each other. The facilities for children to play, and for adults to work together in larger centres are not only inadequate in number but are difficult to provide.
Every time our great democracies have been faced with a challenge involving maximum danger, the people of the nation, having a strong sense of community, have risen, met the challenge, and defeated it. That has been very much the history of Canada. Yet in our larger centres this feeling of community is disappearing. It is disappearing at a time when its strengths and leadership are needed badly.
In my community the Neighbourhood Improvement Program and the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program have worked very well to supply some of the dynamics I have mentioned. The difficulty has been that the programs have not been operative in all our urban areas and have no impact in our rural sections. Marysville, Barker's Point, Nashwaaksis, and some portions of Devon in my community have not qualified for the program at all, or they have qualified for it in a diminished way. Municipal authorities and I have been pressing as hard as possible to have the program expanded into these areas.
The minister announced modifications to the RRAP program as of May 16, 1978. The purpose of the modifications was to make more widely available loans and forgiveness grants based on income. The positive modifications involving elimination of the need to live in a designated area to receive assistance, and the priority to people with low incomes and in areas with housing more in need of repairs, are commendable. The expansion of the list of improvements which may qualify for assistance is a good one. But the elimination of subsidized interest, and the indication that housing co-operatives are no longer eligible for assistance, are negative moves. Over all the modifications represent a net reduction in the government's financial commitments to residential rehabilitation. The total budget for RRAP this year is $9 million, and that really limits it as a universal program.
The new low income housing program announced last May to replace the public housing assistance program, the non-profit housing program, is another good feature. The negative aspects are that the RRAP program and the rent supplement no longer apply to co-op housing. The minimum rent to income rates of 25 per cent may mean that senior citizens, the disabled, and low income earners in public housing projects, will face an increase in their existing rents. Certainly I hope they will not. The interest subsidies do not last for the duration of the projects. They rise with the rental incomes of the property. Thus, with rental incomes increasing as a result of the 25 per cent minimum role, the interest rate after one year probably will accelerate.
The replacement of the Neighbourhood Improvement Program, the municipal infrastructure program and the municipal incentive grant program with the new Community Services

Grant Program, represents the re-organization of existing programs which appear to deal with the same municipal public works aspects as the former programs. But the block funding aspect, through the provincial governments, will have to contemplate the regional disparities which exist in the country, to be effective, or, like so many other federal programs, it will be welcome but not effective in helping to close the gap between the Atlantic provinces and the rest of Canada.
In summary, I find the legislation before us has some good points and some bad ones. The greatest deficiency is its failure to stimulate community services and social programs in our rural areas. There are some stimulating elements and some good program vehicles for our urban centres, but the bottom line is, "You only get what you pay for". The dedication of the government to community life and housing, like the resources it puts into it, is not yet an inspiring record.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the previous speakers and on several occasions I followed the discussion of the bill in the House. I am however rather surprised to note that in our country where we have almost everything such as concrete, lumber and manpower, many unemployed, some carpenters, we often have to tackle housing problems. Considering that we are living in a system which I feel is all wrong, we are trying, I understand, to make the best possible use of a bad condition and this is why we are considering Bill C-29 this evening.
Following many studies and consultations with provincial governments, the Minister of Public Works and Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) had already suggested some amendments to the housing policy of the federal government. Later on, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) announced some budget cuts which required amendments to the National Housing Act.
Amongst those changes, we note that the government, through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, will no longer be a prime lender. It will delegate that task to the private sector. On the other hand, the corporation will guarantee loans of up to a maximum of $40 billion. That figure represents the total amount of loans for which insurance policies will be issued under the act and will absorb part of the interest costs through subsidies. The corporation will be a lender of last resort for public and conventional housing.
In a speech given by the Minister of Public Works and Minister of State for Urban Affairs at the convention of the Quebec Home Builders Association, on November 24, 1978, the government explained its housing policy. First, it would intervene progressively less. We believe that private enterprise can meet the challenge quite well, and meet adequately on its own future needs in the field of conventional housing. Our role will, in the future, be restricted to contributing to the maintenance of a stable market that is competitive and dynamic,
March 12, 1979

without intervening in fields which rightly belong to free enterprise.
Through this bill, the government therefore withdraws from the field of mortgage loans. It will subsidize housing projects of a social nature by reimbursing part of the interest. The government wants to put more money into housing for low-income Canadians and give more responsibility to the private sector in residential financing. Priority will no longer go to housing units intended for the average-income home owner. That will have a bearing on such programs as the assisted home ownership program and the rental housing assistance program since all subsidies are being cut to produce housing for people of average means. However, maximum sale prices under those programs, as well as the maximum guaranteed loans, will be supervised.
The federal government seems to want to simplify the complex workings of federal and provincial community housing and services programs. The administration of joint programs will be simplified thus, in practice, eliminating often costly and inefficient overlapping and duplication. The new non-profit housing program is aimed at the non-profit corporations, be they private, provincial or municipal, and at the non-profit housing co-ops. It is specifically geared towards low-income earners. The government wishes to make this program more attractive for users and to reach a greater number of low-income earners. The goal is the construction or renovation, but especially the renovation, construction being left in the hands of private enterprise, of some 30,000 housing units, compared to the present level of 19,000 units. This is indeed a praiseworthy effort and it is most desirable that these goals be reached. The federal government will be assisting the non-profit housing program through contributions. Eligibility for these contributions and the manner in which these can be allocated under governor in council regulations will be determined by clause 14 of the bill. In practice, the government will pay a large part of the interests charged on money borrowed from the private sector by means of grants, thus reducing the real rate of interest to 1 per cent on loans covering up to 90 per cent of the project's value, and to 2 per cent on loans covering 100 per cent of their value. Both types of loans will be amortized over 35 years.
Furthermore, the government will give subsidies up to $75,000, as a starting fund, to those who want to provide low cost housing, depending on the size and the complexity of the project. It will enable developers to make proposals which may produce viable projects. The accent will be put on the improvement of existing units rather than on the building aspect. Public, co-operative and non-profit units will be offered to low income people, the rent being a percentage, 25 per cent, of incomes or of market rents, whichever solution is the most advantageous. There will be a purchase option for people residing in non-profit and co-operative housing developments, all projects being subject to the standards and regulations of
Housing
the National Housing Act. The federal government will continue to deal directly with co-operative and non-profit organizations. Provincial and municipal non-profit corporations will no longer be under the responsibility of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation as far as selection, review, approval and inspection of the projects are concerned. Instead, the corporation will accept a provincial certificate showing that the requirements of the program have been met in order to determine eligibility for contributions. I will turn to loans and insurances issued by federal authorities, the Corporation's information leaflets. The government will encourage a greater use of the rent supplement program under which the federal and provincial governments support occupancy of a portion of housing units in private sector projects by low income families. Up until now, mortgage insurance was available only for the purchase of a new home. It will now cover the purchase or improvement of a rental housing project and the conversion of a non-residential building into rental housing. Also, certain loans issued by approved lenders will be 100 per cent insurable. This policy will apply to non-profit corporations wanting to buy, improve, build or modify rental housing projects or home or pension type housing facilities, and also to co-operative housing associations wanting to buy, build or modify housing projects.
For the first time, private sector lenders will issue and insure loans to residents of Indian reserves, whether to an idividual or to an Indian band or group, but only with the approval of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner). In this case, Indians are as defined by the Indian Act. This loan may serve for the building or rehabilitation of reserve housing. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation used to lend money to owner-lessors. In view of CMHC's new policy of opting out of the loans market, loans issued by the private sector to owner-lessors, under the residential rehabilitation aid program, will be insurable. Under clause 15, lenders will be able to obtain a rapid settlement of loans insured under the National Housing Act, in cases of default.
Clause 4 provides that insured loans can be made to co-operatives provided the majority of units are occupied or owned by the members or shareholders of the co-operative. Previously, 80 per cent occupation or ownership was required. Under clause 1, the corporation could insure certain loans based on other securities than a first mortgage. That security could be note for a second mortgage or any other security depending on the size of the loan. Clause 2 says that loans made or guaranteed by provincial governments under this law will be exempt for mortgage insurance fees. Let us remember that the total amount of all mortgage loans the corporation will be able to insure will go from $25 billion to $40 billion. The essence of the changes with respect to the rehabilitation program is contained in clause 7.

March 12, 1979
Housing
Private sector financing is made available to owners, nonprofit corporations and Indians as amended by clause 7. Furthermore, the need for designated areas is eliminated. All restrictions are set aside or withdrawn. As a result of the budget restrictions of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, loans will no longer be made to landlords for rehabilitation purposes. They will have to get their loans from the private sector. As previously stated, these loans will be insurable under the act.
Clause 8 suppresses the limit of $500 per unit on the rehabilitation on homes for the elderly or boarding-house types of housing facilities. That program helps landlords or nonprofit co-operatives and associations. For an occupying owner, this assistance comes in the form of a loan which may be forgiven altogether. The maximum loan is $10,000. The borrower whose adjusted family income does not exceed $6,000 is entitled to a loan forgiveness of up to $3,750. If the adjusted family income is $ 11,000 or more, the loan must be paid back in full. Owners of rental housing can obtain loans of up to $10,000 per housing unit. Payment of 50 per cent of the loan, up to a maximum amount of $2,500 per housing unit, can be forgiven if the owner consents to rent control. Non-profit organizations can also obtain loans of up to $10,000 in which case forgiveness of payment goes up to maximum of $3,750. New projects involving purchase and repairs are not eligible under this program. When the assistance is granted for the creation or the improvement of the hostel or dormitory type of housing, this assistance can represent up to $4,000 per bed, of which payment of $500 can be forgiven.
There is also the graduated payment mortgages program. Clause 5 introduces the notion of graduated payment mortgages, which is rather complex. This aims at simplifying the acquisition of low-cost housing. What is it exactly? Simply an ordinary mortgage for which the monthly charges start at a relatively low level and go up progressively until they reach a certain ceiling. I have here some evidence about this type of graduated payment mortgages. Of course, this concerns public housing, or low-cost housing projects, and it involves a loan of $1,487,700 for the construction of a public housing building. I see here that the residents of the community where this project is being built will have to pay $5,856,206.32 in interests alone in a 50-year period. The amount that they owe is $1,487,700. This is what we must watch out for in graduated payment mortgages.
The payments for the principal and the interest charges of a graduated payment mortgage start at a lower level than for a conventional mortgage. However, these monthly charges will increase by 5 per cent a year until the end of the tenth year. They will then stabilize at this level for the rest of the repayment period, which means that during the first years of repayment of a graduated payment mortgage, you are not paying current interests on the borrowed capital.

This will increase the total debt on a 1014 per cent rate, $35,000 mortgage with 25 year term by $10,000, as compared to a fixed payment mortgage. If this be an advantage, this system will allow earlier ownership. So here is the option: Earlier ownership with a $10,000 larger indebtedness, or later ownership with more money in the pocket. Is it really worth it to get lower debt because one is anxious to own a house?
The difficulty, as always, is borrowing. There are a lot of poor people who have difficulty in obtaining a loan, and interest charges are much too high. If we calculate payments the owner will have to make in 20, 25 or 30 years from now, we often find he will have to pay the cost of two or three houses before he can get out of debt.
The only amendment to the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation Act in part two of Bill C-29 is the change of name to "Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation." This comes within the Canadianization program of the federal government, and is aimed at stressing that the corporation is an arm of the Canadian government. Unless the minister is planning early amendments to payment arrangements with reduced interest rates, a better name in the circumstances would be "Canadian Mortgage and Debt Corporation," because the loans help getting people into debt for years to come. I have here ample evidence of that.
The housing co-operatives had this to say about the new federal housing programs: "The new federal housing programs are aimed at helping builders start with hard-to-sell houses rather than assuring the construction of a larger number of units": Le Droit, May 25, 1978. It will be remembered the federal government wants to stress renovation rather than construction. Co-operatives would therefore be "forced to use existing buildings rather than building new ones. Some buildings could not be sold because of poor design or poor location". Should it become almost impossible to build we must expect that people interested in co-operatives, as they make the management of building projects possible, will no longer be interested in that type of organization.
The CMHC is asking for total control over housing co-operatives by establishing in advance the type of restoration and the cost of rent. Those "electorally profitable austerity programs" make a complete farce of voluntary participation of members, one of the basis of co-operatives. The complete loss of autonomy is one of the most discouraging aspects for co-operatives. On November 13 1978, a press release from the Quebec City housing co-operatives urged the government to give priority to the needs of co-operatives by establishing special programs. According to that press release, the government should put directly at their disposal all funds required to finance their projects at a preferential rate compare to that of the private sector.
Housing co-operatives want tenant-co-operators to pay no more than 20 per cent of their gross income instead of 25 per cent as proposed by the government; that interests rates for
March 12, 1979

mortgage loans be fixed instead of variable; that housing co-operatives do not offer purchase options as it is a co-operative of tenants. The government, through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, changes its position by supporting totally co-operative housing and abandoning the private housing market to concentrate on housing for low wage earners.
The Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, RRAP, will mostly benefit Quebec: nearly 45 per cent of the $145 million earmarked for this program will be allocated to Quebec which is showing the deepest desire to rehabilitate its old houses. But the minister has been accused in this House of operating for electoral purposes in promising to expand housing programs whereas the government does not have the funds needed to implement them.
Indeed, ministerial advisers are concerned over the shortage of funds needed to meet demands under the promised expanded housing rehabilitation program. Moreover, the RRAP program is likely to change housing conditions in Quebec; but if money is not available, this might become an electoral commitment without foundation since the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program actually is almost starved of public funds.
Evidently, any housing rehabilitation program in Canada becomes a monetary problem in this unsettled financial system of ours. We have all the material required; millions of well disposed workers now without a job and many families who need decent housing. But too often budgetary restraints forbid construction. This results from a broken down financial system which we should change soon as it brings about many useless complications that, in my opinion, could be avoided.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have entered the debate on Bill C-29. I have followed with great interest the proceedings prior to second reading, during second reading, at report stage, and now at third reading. I enter the debate at this late hour because of a number of events which have transpired throughout the handling of this bill. There are two specific areas that have not received the attention they should, namely, the problem of housing as it relates to the native community, specifically the Indian and Inuit people; and also as it relates to senior citizens. In my view this bill does not address itself to these areas in a responsible or adequate manner.
From the outset the minister has been toying or playing political games with the provinces and municipalities. 1 say that because the minister has refused until this late date to introduce this important bill. This is legislation which required far more time, not only at second reading but during committee stage, report stage, and again at third reading.
The minister knows perfectly well there are provinces and municipalities all across Canada which have been acting in
Housing
good faith in arranging programs. They have been waiting for this legislation to be introduced and passed so they could proceed with the programs they had been contemplating and hoping to have implemented within a reasonable period of time.
1 find that an interesting scenario. The minister has travelled across Canada and made important pronouncements about this program. He has prodded and encouraged municipalities and provinces to go ahead with plans for various programs. Then he delays the introduction of this legislation for almost a year. As I indicated, we have had very little time to debate what I consider are some important aspects of the bill. We have not had an opportunity to enlarge on various areas of housing which this party considers extremely important.
Notwithstanding some important elements in the legislation one has to ask the question, why would the minister follow this particular course of action? Why would he talk about this legislation for over a year and then introduce it at the last moment at a time when this House could dissolve imminently? There are probably several reasons for this. The minister is aware of numerous horror stories within that department and I am sure he is aware of various allegations that have been made with regard to the mismanagement of funds, possible patronage and corruption that have existed within that department and various programs. Of course this is not uncommon in other areas of government.
The minister knows there are certain aspects of this legislation that are inconsistent with his public pronouncements. These have been questioned by different segments of our community. I will not go into those, Mr. Speaker, because my colleagues have covered a number of them in the past. However, I feel there are specific areas of housing which have been virtually ignored in this debate.
For a moment or two I would like to talk about senior citizens and the importance of housing to them, and the inadequacy of housing for the native population, specifically the Indian and the Inuit people across Canada.
It is important to put in perspective the extent of mismanagement and misappropriation of funds which are the responsibility of the minister responsible for this bill. It is important for at least three reasons. I am sure there are others, but there are three that I want to emphasize. Initially it reconfirms the position that has been expressed by this party on numerous occasions regarding the excesses of this government, its mismanagement and fiscal irresponsiblity in handling programs. I would suggest that if they were eliminated that could be done without impairing services to Canadians. That is not a partisan position.
I recall being at the public accounts committee hearing when the Auditor General made his report in November, 1978. In issue number five of the minutes of the public accounts committee for November 23, 1978, at page 5:21, the Auditor General, in response to a question regarding the principle of value for money, said:

Indeed if the mismanagement that has been demonstrated in so many programs under the auspices of this minister were removed, the services could be provided to Canadians rather than seeing so many programs cut back or eliminated. I will give some examples of this in a moment.
I must mention also that many of these horror stories associated with the ministry unfortunately have been perceived to be related to the failure of innocent victims. This is not new in this House of Commons. I am sure members in this House will recall that two years ago at the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development we discussed the Indian economic development fund. We demonstrated during an opposition day in this House that there had been at least $50 million mismanaged by that particular department for this one program. Yet the impression was left that it was the Indian community in Canada that had failed. I suggest that same ingredient exists for similar programs that have been handled under this ministry.
Because of the government's inability and its failure to administer programs in an adequate way, it has become immobilized and it has actually become paralysed with respect to many programs and it has lost the ability to govern in that respect. Let us take a look at one department as an example. A moment ago I mentioned the program of Indian economic development, and the government's mismanagement of it. That was confirmed in the Auditor General's 1978 report. What has happend since that time? The entire program of economic development which we consider crucial to Indian problems across Canada has virtually been ignored and there is no program in that sense of the word.
The Indian arts and crafts control marketing service, a program which I consider to be outstanding as an outlet for Indian arts and crafts across the country, was terminated by this government at the end of last year because of its mismanagement of the program. I can assure you that that project will be pursued very actively when the estimates are before the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Again, there have been cutbacks on health care to Indian and Inuit people across Canada. Perhaps I could put this in its best perspective by relating a brief part of a conversation I had with the Nova Scotia Indian Brotherhood about two weeks ago. They were talking about the delivery of services to the various reserves and settlements in that province. They came up with a very interesting figure which they could document. It showed that the federal government is spending $8 to deliver 75 cents worth of services to the Indian people on those reserves and in those communities. That is the type of problem about which I am talking. It is the type of issue that has been ignored throughout the debate.

As I indicated earlier, the implications of this legislation virtually ignore senior citizens across the country. I will come back to that in a moment or two. A number of my colleagues have gone into the horror stories with regard to this program over the years. I mention in passing the problems with York Place and similar projects of that nature such as the luxurious hotels, something that is common knowledge to all hon. members of this House.
I was most interested in a brochure with regard to one of them. It describes, and I quote:
-the ambience throughout Hotel Le Quai d'Orsay is most distinctive and reflects the mood of 20th century aristocratic living.
I can assure hon. members the people I am speaking for and talking about, the senior citizens across this country, certainly those in my area, and the native people, are not interested in aristocratic living. They simply want a roof over their heads and reasonable homes in which to live. I will come to those statistics in a moment.
My colleagues talked about the disasters in the area of AHOP and the graduated mortgage program. I was most impressed with the five-part series published by the Hamilton Spectator during the period January 27 to February 1, 1979, regarding the disasters with respect to CMHC. I have no intention of quoting extensively, but there are two of extreme interest to me because they relate to two of the issues I referred to earlier. One was "$500,000 for 12 basements". The other issue was entitled "RCMP Probing Housing Disaster, Sutton Project Cost Us $300,000". Those two projects relate to the rural and native housing program. As I indicated before, it demonstrates the mismanagement on the part of this government, the misappropriation and misallocation of funds. Because of that this government has not been able to live up to its mandate to provide the type of housing that is needed in this area.
I want to make a comment or two about senior citizens' housing. I must be honest. I am not impressed nor am 1 convinced that the legislation before us is responsive to that particular need across Canada. Why is it important? I had the fortunate opportunity before coming to the House of Commons of dealing to a great extent with senior citizens across Canada, particularly in my area. Senior citizens are not really a demanding group. However, if there is one aspect that stands out when dealing with senior citizens it is the problem of loneliness. It is probably the single most important medical problem they face.
Senior citizens are interested people. They want to remain in their own homes, near their families and in their community among their friends. I recently attended a ninetieth birthday which demonstrated this in a most eloquent and sensitive way.
I knew this individual who was celebrating her ninetieth birthday. How wonderful it was that the entire family could be at this nursing home to celebrate it with her. The sensitivity was experienced by all of us. It was not only felt by her family and those friends around her, but by all the inhabitants of that small community. This is a very important aspect.
