The reeve of a small village in my area wrote to me in January after hearing about this bill. He was concerned that senior citizen housing would not be available for the small village of Thamesville. 1 quote from his letter:
Council learned from the Ministry of Housing that the village would have to form a chartered public non-profit making organization. Ninety per cent of the capital funds would have to be raised privately just to be eligible for rent subsidies. We would also be responsible for planning and carrying out the project ourselves with only the advice of the Ministry of Housing.
I talked to the reeve of that small village of about 1,000 about this problem. I simply draw to the attention of hon. members the last portion "responsible for planning and carrying out the project ourselves". As I said, this is a small village of about 1,000 people. Do they have an architect? Do they have individuals who can do the type of planning that might be done in metro Toronto or some other large city? That involves a very substantial cost for a town of that size. The government did not address itself to that in this legislation.
I have received letters from that and other communities wherein senior citizens have reflected on the problems and the necessity of our addressing ourselves to those problems. 1 quote from one letter:
-we understand they found $ 18 million to help four cities with hockey arenas. Is this more important than having shelter for the people that played a large part in the building of this country .. . Every year we have seniors that have to leave their larger homes or farms and friends and go to other centres to find shelter. This is very upsetting to older people.
Another woman wrote to say she had lost four friends in the last year. They moved to larger centres because of the absence of senior citizen housing in that area.
I know my time is running out, but I must say a few words about the problem of Indian housing across Canada. I suppose this could be best demonstrated by the experience in Assumption. I am sure hon. members are cognizant of what has appeared on the national news and in newspapers across Canada with regard to the fact there have been at least three deaths in the past two weeks of infants in that small community, due to bronchialitis, which is related to substandard housing in that community. This can be documented across the country.
On our allotted day on November 18, 1976, this party outlined in a very responsible manner the problems related to housing for Indian and native people across this country. Let me just take a moment or two to give some indication of the severity of that problem. On that day we talked about the Indians, the Inuit and, indeed, the native problem itself.
As I recall, today is the fifth anniversary of the rural and native housing program and of the government's commitment to build 50,000 homes for that community. How many homes have actually been built during that period? Not more than
7,000,	plus or minus one or two hundred. On the anniversary date, a government which talks about a positive housing policy for the Indians and Inuit has built less than 1,000 homes during the whole five-year period. It is estimated that over a period of 30 years, 31,000 houses were built for Indians; of
Housing
that number 14,000 were considered substandard in 1976, 9,000 required rehabilitation on a major scale, and more than 7,500 were beyond repair. The figures have not improved. If anything they are worse today, and there is nothing in the bill before us which addresses itself to this problem. Ten per cent of those homes consisted of no more than one room, often with ten to 15 individuals crowding into it.
Seventy per cent of the Indian population were without water, 25 per cent were forced to use water known to be contaminated, and 40 per cent had to rely on surface water- imagine the health hazards there. Ninety per cent had to use outside pit toilets for sewage disposal.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on and on describing conditions in the Inuit community. The situation in the Inuit community is no better. We know there were buildings put up in the north in the southern style, which virtually disintegrated over a five-year period. They were unsuited to the lifestyle of those who lived in them and were inconsistent with climatic conditions in the northern regions. Fifty thousand homes were promised five years ago, and only 7,000 were delivered, as I have stated, under the government's native policy.
I can recall bringing the attention of the House to the seriousness of this problem on an earlier occasion, while this subject was under debate on November 18, 1976. I can recall the minister's comments on that day. If I may say so, he demonstrated no interest in native housing policy on that occasion; he was more concerned about other matters. To show the seriousness of the problem let me quote from page 1145 of Hansard for November 18, 1976:
In many areas houses are so worthless that residents seldom bother to spend money on improvements or make an effort to repair them. Broken windows are patched with cardboard boxes.
Rusty cream cans are used for water storage. It is rare if there is more than one bed and more than one or two chairs. When a visitor eats at home he usually is given the few dishes and silverware, while the family eats out of the tin pans or even tin cans. Most homes have electricity. Kerosene lamps are the only source of light. In many communities, water is scarce and has to be hauled long distances. Often it is unfit for human consumption.
I could go on. However, I entered the debate at this late stage primarily because of my grave concern, my feeling that the government and the minister have ignored two extremely important areas as far as housing is concerned. I am not satisfied that there has been a positive response from the government to the needs of senior citizens, and I am not satisfied that the government has demonstrated any interest in native housing in Canada or developed any policy to deal with it.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have an opportunity to rise for the first time in this debate. I expected to participate earlier, but because of the tragedy of miners being killed in my riding I had to spend a much longer period of time than I anticipated down home in connection with that terrible catastrophe as well as with other problems.
I browsed through the Debates so far because that is really all I had time to do. The minister seemed preoccupied in his lengthy speech in this debate with dispelling the idea of a housing crisis in Canada. At this late hour I do not want to get into a semantic discussion because I want to give at least one member of the official opposition five or seven minutes. However, whether we call it a crisis or not, the situation is close to a crisis by anybody's definition except, evidently, the minister's. CMHC figures as recently as last year indicated that approximately 1,225,000 households in this country are suffering from some form of housing deprivation. This breaks down into 180,000 families living in inadequate dwellings, 298,000 overcrowded dwellings, and 547,000 families paying more than 25 per cent of their total income on shelter. These are dry statistics, but they have a very serious meaning for the human beings involved. What I am saying is that a million households being affected means that several million Canadians are affected by these conditions, and if that is not a crisis it is something of which this country should be ashamed.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) quoted Mr. Teron's speech in Calgary of two years ago, which is an additional piece of evidence from CMHC despite the seemingly loose connection Mr. Teron still has with CMHC or what is to be called "the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation" because of these amendments. In November of 1976 Mr. Teron said and I quote, "that when 280,000 families in Canada pay more than 50 per cent of their family income for housing"-and that is shocking to me-"550,000 families in Canada pay more than 45 per cent." Imagine that in this day of high food prices and high prices for everything else. Imagine shelling out that kind of money for housing. Mr. Teron said that 820,000 families at that time paid more than 25 per cent, and two thirds of Canadians in need of housing could not afford to buy or rent without a subsidy from their fellow man. He said that we had a fundamental problem. Whether in the minister's mind we have a crisis or not, we certainly have a fundamental problem. Mr. Teron went on to say that, and I quote, "we must take reasonable action now or more drastic action later".
In connection with one part of this whole housing problem I want to pick up the theme of Mr. Teron when he referred to a national housing crisis. The minister might use some other word. With regard to the national housing problem which besets this country I want to speak of one element which relates to my home constituency. I have been dealing with the minister on this for some two years and with his predecessor before that. This problem relates to the inability of the Resi-
March 12, 1979

dential Rehabilitation Assistance Program and the Neighbourhood Improvement Program to do certain jobs in certain areas.
In the mining towns which make up a major part of my constituency some housing is 70 to 100 years old. Marx and nineteenth century socialists would call this housing proletarian housing. Private companies have dug pits and built coal mines, and built houses around them. Around these pits or collieries, as they are called in other countries, people were crowded into company housing. After these companies get their money out, they leave. I do not want to digress too far, but the only country in the world which has a real private mining industry is the United States. To me it is no coincidence that United States mines have had over the years the worst safety features of all in the western world and, as far as we know, even parts of eastern Europe such as Poland which is light years ahead of the United States in that respect. I say that by way of digression. However, there is an essential problem.
I am not saying that the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, even in these mining areas, has not been good, because it has. However, the program has been slow and cumbersome. I have correspondence here which dates back to the time I came here. This correspondence is with one minister after another. It deals with Devco, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), the former minister of housing now the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson), and others. This correspondence shows that all of them, including CMHC and Devco, ran around the problem and continually told me that there were other programs or that they could not get into this type of thing.
CMHC told me that it did not want to initiate action. I feel that CMHC is not flexible enough. I do not say that about local officials, but I do say that about policy-making and its application. I agree with the fundamental argument of our party-and I push it forward-that we want centralization of the monetary and fiscal policies of this country to remain in federal hands. If the federal government does not want to give the provinces a bigger share in the management of housing policy within their regions it could at least be more flexible in application with regard to its universal program in areas like mine, and, for example, Sudbury and Timmins which have old housing. This old housing is the legacy of these areas, and it is the worst part of their past. Something should be done to correct that.
I suggested to the minister, CMHC and Devco, that in an area of high unemployment rehabilitation should be promoted. That rehabilitation should be for the benefit of senior citizens and widows who are now living in much of this older housing. It should be made better for them. I suggested that would be a real investment in the future and that it would reduce the amount of new construction for public housing and senior citizens housing. I proposed a special rehabilitation agency for an area like Cape Breton. I have been kept dancing around by these Crown corporations and these ministers on this issue because they just have not been able to co-ordinate or did not have the will to do so. They have not been flexible, and no

initiative has been taken to correct the serious deficiencies in the areas to which I referred.
The reason I am so upset about this is that this year RRAP does not include something which may not seem important to some members of this House but which is very important to a member like me, that is, that no foundations are to be included under RRAP this year. I have been asking for a new rehabilitation agency, and that foundations be put under what were formerly company houses now owned by miners since the post-war period, lived in by miners, pensioners, widows, and low income people. I would like this housing to be upgraded by the addition of foundations. We have come to the conclusion it would cost about $8,000 per household. I asked the present head of Devco, who was then interim head, Mr. Steve Rankin, to try to get CMHC going on this and to use the growth component of the Canada Works program, but again things are so slow there, and the explanations given to MPPs are so inadequate that it is difficult to get any of these things off the ground.
I appeal to the minister tonight to tell CMHC officials in Sydney, "Look we have taken in people from Kentucky", which they did. We held meetings and we found there are no parallels whatsoever between the problem in Kentucky and the housing problem in our mining areas and former mining areas, including the area where our Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) was born. We could take 60 houses as a pilot project at $8,000 each, which comes to roughly $480,000. With the present delivery system, we could put foundations under these houses and people could contribute something small out of their incomes, which would come to roughly only $7,300 on average. subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EQUAL OPPORTUNITY FOR WOMEN IN PUBLIC SERVICE
STATUS OF WOMEN-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EQUAL OPPORTUNITY FOR WOMEN IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped a moment ago until the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) left the chamber that he was going to be here to reply to this question, because for over a year now I have been attempting to get some firm accounting from the minister in respect of the treatment by the government of its female employees in the public service. I hope, in the course of the next few minutes, to remind the minister, whether he is here tonight or has the opportunity to read this later, of the very serious allegations and criticisms which are contained in the latest report of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women regarding the situation of women in the public service.
As members will know, in January of this year the Advisory Council on the Status of Women issued again, as it has done on an annual basis in recent years, a report on the progress

women have made in the public service. This report is entitled "Barriers to Equal Opportunity." I believe that this report is a veritable catalogue of discriminations and failures on the part of the government in acting on behalf of its female public employees.
As the report states clearly in its introduction, the government's direct responsibility regarding the employment of women is crucial because, as the report sets out at page 1:
First, as the largest single employer of women, it has a direct responsibility to provide equal opportunities for women in the public service.
That is a mandate and a responsibility which very clearly, as this report indicates, has not been lived up to. The government increasingly has treated women as a reserve pool of labour.
I do not have time this evening to point out all the detail, but I would be delighted to hear the minister's response in explaining how it is that as income difficulties have grown, as the report says at page 13, "the federal government, in its employment practices continues to treat women as if they constitute a reserve pool of labour".
I hope in the course of the next few minutes to point out very clearly how, again and again, this report indicts the government in terms of its responsibilities in respect of the employment of women in the public service.
At page 15, in terms of the situation regarding term appointments, one indication of the attitude that has actually been lived up to regarding the public service is stated in the report:
As of March 1978, 17 per cent of public servants were employed on a term basis. Approximately half of these employees were men and half women.
On the surface that would appear quite fair, as the report states. It goes on to state that the facts are that "fewer women are public servants." The report states:
As of March 1978, only 36.7 per cent of public servants, including seasonal and term employees, were women.
The tendency to place women in term appointments is growing, not diminishing. The percentage of term employees who were women increased from 45.2 per cent in 1976 to 48.7 per cent in 1977-
Further on at page 20 of this report it is pointed out with regard to the over-all improvement women have made in the public service:
Moreover, there has been little improvement over time. If we compare the 1977 quintile breakdown with quintile figures for 1973 and 1975, we find that the distribution has changed only minimally.
Further on it points out:
In the middle quintile, there was a reversal in 1977 of an upward trend between 1973 and 1975.
In respect of the recent lay-offs that have been taking place, and I think here we are reminded of some exchanges which took place between my colleague, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan), the report points out at page 23:
Between 1976 and 1977 the number of public servants laid off more than doubled from 1012 to 2347. In 1976, 470, or 46 per cent of the employees laid off were women. In 1977, 1243 women were laid off, representing 53 per cent of the total. This increase is shocking enough in itself, but when we remember that
March 12, 1979

women account for only 37 per cent of federal public servants, the discrimination becomes even more glaring.
Hon. members may recall that a number of questions were raised in this House a year ago about the number of women entering the career assignment program and about those achieving appointments in the upper and middle levels of management in the public service. On page 31 the report says:
Even in this program, the representation of women has dropped. Although, as the table below confirms, in 1975 women accounted for 30.6 per cent of the participants in the CAP, by 1977 they accounted for only 14 per cent falling behind the 1973 representation.
Finally, this part of the report concludes with a summation of the report that has been presented to the government. On page 44 it says:
The preceding statistics reveal that the federal government has failed to provide equal opportunities for women in the public service.
It goes on to point out that instead of being ahead of the private sector, it is trailing behind. Why is this? Why has there been this failure?
On page 46 the report points out:
-the government's failure to address the basic patterns which underly the historic inequality of women.
In effect the report recognizes that the government has not come to grips with the basic elements that would require adjustment or change if real discrimination were to be removed. The report points out on page 52:
Notably absent have been any concrete moves to make the recommended structural adjustments or to actively recruit women into occupational groups where they are under-represented.
It goes on to say at page 53:
It would appear then that inherent in the very programs designed to promote equal opportunities for women is either an unawareness of the historical factors maintaining the inequality or an inability or unwillingness to adopt an employment approach that can address the real issues.
This is the crux of the matter, Mr. Speaker, "an inability or unwillingness" to address the essential structure requires to end discrimination in employment in the public service. I hope that one of the parliamentary secretaries here this evening can give us some concrete reason why the government to this point is only prepared to dismiss a highly important and helpful report.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EQUAL OPPORTUNITY FOR WOMEN IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member will understand that in the three minutes afforded to me this evening it will be impossible to provide any kind of thesis or in depth response to the argument he makes relying on the report he has quoted so copiously. It will afford me, however, the opportunity at least to deal with a couple of the points he raised at some length and with some vigour. He suggests that the lay-offs taking place and the figures on which he relied, were shocking.
I would point out, as has the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) in response to questions put by the hon. member and others on that side of the House with respect to lay-offs, and "the last hired, first fired" statement that was
Adjournment Debate
made, that in fact those persons hired most recently are those who might be expected to be laid off first. Short of coming out with some kind of hybrid whereby there would be no opportunity for those with tenure enjoying more job security than those most recently hired, it would seem to be impossible, with a large influx of women into the labour market, not to have a disproportionately large number of them laid off when such large lay-offs take place.
The government has indicated that the argument may not be acceptable in terms of what is actually taking place. The difficulty we are dealing with is structural. When there is a larger influx of women, as has been the case in recent days, it might be expected that they would be the first to go when lay-offs take place.
In the time remaining perhaps I might be permitted to indicate by way of history that a cabinet directive No. 44 issued in 1972 requested that deputy heads of departments promote women in middle and upper echelon positions. Since that time numbers of women have been increasing in all categories except scientific and professional. The 1975 cabinet directive stated that every deputy head must assign an officer responsible for the EOW program. That has happened. I should like to be able to present more facts and figures but 1 am restricted by the time available.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-SETTLEMENT WITH UNION TO AVOID FURTHER DETERIORATION OF AIR SAFETY
AIR TRANSPORT-SETTLEMENT WITH UNION TO AVOID FURTHER DETERIORATION OF AIR SAFETY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with every department head having at least three female secretaries, why shouldn't what the parliamentary secretary has said be true notwithstanding what my colleague has just referred to?
My concern tonight is the plight facing air travellers in Canada. In particular it refers to a question which I raised on February 5, well over a month ago, respecting negotiations between the department and the air inspectors and their bargaining procedures. It seems six weeks after the question was raised that negotiations are in limbo, and while this is so there is a continuing demoralization of these individuals. Without question there is a lowering of the capacity of these people to apply themselves vigorously to their jobs and responsibilities.
Continuously in this House in recent months there has been a plea from the opposition for the government to move swiftly to remove any cause for concern on the part of those who use aircraft to travel across Canada. I sugest there is a failure on the part of the government to recognize that beyond the bargaining procedures there is a responsibility to make absolutely certain that there is no cause for fear or alarm among the air travelling public.
Failure of the government to do this prompted me to ask once again this evening if the parliamentary secretary could indicate the status of the negotiations. Could he tell us whether the principle of comparability, so eloquently espoused by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) has

March 12, 1979
Adjournment Debate
found favour among his colleagues on the Treasury benches? If so, as a result of that, can we anticipate any action on the part of the government to reopen the talks which seem to be somewhat stalemated at the moment? These are essentially the questions that concern us. We cannot continue to have a high standard maintained if the people who are asked to do the job are not anywhere nearly comparable in wages to those with similar training in the private sector. I will not dwell on that topic, but I am sure the parliamentary secretary appreciates and understands the implications of it.
Let me remind the parliamentary secretary once more, if I may, that the question of safety in transport, and the conflicts which arise therefrom, are not a new subject in this House. I can tell him that I have had a private member's bill prepared for his edification, and I know he has looked at it, which gets to the root of the problem when the regulatory agency continues to have to accept responsibility for the investigated or consequential result of that regulatory authority posed in a statutory manner. These things must come to an end, the charade like that which arose out of Cranbrook, with the attempt by the ministry to bury a report until such time as they have had a chance to prepare new regulations, authorities and tighter and tougher rules with regard to air safety. That is not good enough. The minister should look at his internal organization in the hope that the ultimate beneficiary will be the travelling public in this country.
I am a minor individual. However, 1 have just completed my 1,300th trip between this city and my city of Halifax. 1 am not unfamiliar with aircraft. When I board an aeroplane I like to know that the highest standards possible are in effect. We have the capacity and the trained personnel in this country. They are ready to work. What we need is an awareness and attitude on the part of this government to ensure that our air inspection officers are able to work to their fullest capacity and with the best interests of all Canadians uppermost in their minds. I repeat my question.

subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-HEALTH CARE OF NATIVE PEOPLES
HEALTH AND WELFARE-HEALTH CARE OF NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you may recall that late last fall, around Christmas time and early in January, there was an outcry from the Indian people because the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) had decided to withdraw certain health services from those people. The guidelines which she imposed at that time were based on a broad accusation that Indian people were abusing certain of the health services, particularly ambulance services, dental services, optometric services, and the use of prescription drugs. She made this broad accusation but to this date I have not heard from her one specific example of such abuse.

March 12, 1979

It seems to me that the minister, who poses or attempts to pose before the public as a humane lady, chose on this occasion to attack the poor and the weak-as we all know, the Indians in this country are, by and large, poor and certainly economically speaking, weak. As to their physical state, when we examine the statistics we see that the mortality rate for Indian children is much higher than the rate for the rest of the population; the life expectancy generally is much lower, and in many aspects of life the Indians are falling behind the rest of society. Thus it seems to me that it was a callous decision on the part of the minister to impose these guidelines which make it more difficult, if not impossible, for sick Indian people to get ambulance drives to hospital or to obtain the drugs they require, sometimes on an emergency basis. But she acted on the basis of a broad accusation that people were abusing the system.
As a result of representations from members of my party, the National Indian Brotherhood and other Indian organizations, she did, however, agree to suspend these guidelines for a six-month period. She explained she was doing so in order to have more time in which to consult with Indian people. Mr. Speaker, the fact is that so far she refuses even to talk with them. She has refused to set in motion any mechanism for the consultation process in which she told us she wanted to engage.
In support of this statement, I should like to read a telex which was sent to the minister by the National Indian Brotherhood. I may say I had a conversation with the president of the National Indian Brotherhood and the president of the Alberta Indian Association just this afternoon, so the information I have is very current. The telex reads:
It is unfortunate that you feel it is not applicable at this time to discuss the issue of health services and in particular the consultation mechanism established on January 24. You have my letter of January 28 outlining our concerns with the consultation mechanism. We have had no reply. My staff has been in contact with your office no less than eight times since January 24 attempting to set up a meeting with you to clarify the ongoing issue of health services to Indian people. The consultation process appears to be actually negating discussion and we have an executive council meeting and I am sorry I have to report that once again you have refused to meet to discuss and clarify the ongoing health issue.
It appears that the minister is stonewalling. It appears that her promise to negotiate was nothing more than a political ploy to take this issue out of public discussion until the election is over. It is quite clear that she has no intention whatsoever to carry out her promise to negotiate.
Another aspect concerns me very much insofar as her attitude is concerned. At the meeting of January 24 a representative of the National Indian Brotherhood presented the minister with a blanket as a token of esteem. It was a new Hudson Bay blanket. It was a very expensive and very good blanket. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, if you think back, you will realize that it was a very nice gift for the National Indian Brotherhood to offer the minister.
The minister took the blanket, but the next day she had the gall to telephone the president of the National Indian Brotherhood to inquire whether the blanket carried disease or whether there was a curse on it to harm her in any way. The response
Adjournment Debate
the National Indian Brotherhood gave the minister was that it was given to her with only the best intentions and that the minister could send it to her own laboratories to determine whether it carried any disease. I am astonished by the attitude of the minister. It seems quite clear that she has either been badly advised or has committed herself with less than the best of intentions as far as negotiations are concerned. If it was her intention to get past the election with this ploy and if the universe unfolds as it should, my party will pick up the pieces, the consultation process will indeed continue when the election is over, and a humane way will be found to solve this very serious problem.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-HEALTH CARE OF NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I deplore the suggestion of the hon. member that the minister attempted to use as a ploy for time an extension of six months with a view to escaping any obligation she undertook. I think this House and those who know the minister know that she is an honourable woman, and if she gave any undertaking she will indeed seek to do everything possible to fulfil it. I reject out of hand any suggestion by the hon. member that anything other than that is the case.
In addition, I suggest that the hon. member has used the late show to go rather far afield from the question he initially put. If he expects a response to a question he put earlier, he should restrict himself to that question so that any preparation for the purpose of making a response is directed to the initial question.
In any event, at the January 24 meeting the minister did meet with Indian participants who presented their views with regard to the department's guidelines regarding the provision of certain uninsured health services to Indian and Inuit people. I would like to take some time to outline the demands of the Indian people, but the time goes quickly. I can only say that on January 24 the minister indicated that primary health services and programs for Indian people on reserves would not be affected.
The minister explained the reasons for implementing guidelines for uninsured services, which include the provision of eyeglasses, dentures, prescription drugs, and transportation of patients for medical reasons. I think it is important that I state once again that, contrary to the incorrect information the hon. member opposite put on the record, the services we are talking about are not insured services, they are uninsured services. This is not a new policy which was implemented just recently by this government. It is a continuation of the policy which has existed since 1958 and which was put in place by the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker). In fact this is not something that is new and different.
What the minister has indicated is that in fact there had been some abuses that had grown into the system and that, as a consequence, it was time for a rationalization of the system to ensure that proper insured services would be provided under the policy. Notwithstanding the fact that there was a rationalization, because of the misapprehension and misinformation

that had crept into the debate she provided a six months' suspension so that there could be a further discussion and a further understanding of what was going on. She outlined at that time four guidelines or criteria which were made known to the Indian and Inuit representatives at that meeting. I can provide those guidelines to the hon. member again this evening, if he does not have them yet or does not understand them, and I will be pleased to bring all hon. members up to
date on the implementation of the policy pertaining to the health of the Indian and Inuit people, but I see that my time has expired.
